A new study has found that organic food contains more antioxidants and lower levels of toxic metals and pesticides than regular food. The researchers, led by Professor Carlo Leifert at Newcastle University, analyzed 343 studies from around the world to come to this conclusion. They suggest that eating organic fruit and vegetables could have similar health benefits to adding one or two portions of the recommended daily intake.

The study found that organic food contains between 19% and 69% more antioxidants than regular food. Antioxidants are compounds that can help prevent chronic diseases such as heart disease, neurodegenerative diseases, and certain cancers. The researchers also found that conventional crops contain higher levels of cadmium, a toxic metal, and pesticide residues.

The team behind the study believes that these findings could be significant for human nutrition. However, not everyone agrees with their conclusions. Tom Sanders, a professor of nutrition at King's College London, says that the differences between organic and regular food may not be as significant as they seem. He also points out that organic cereals contain less protein than conventional crops.

The study was funded by the EU and an organic farming charity. The researchers acknowledge that their findings could be criticized for including too many studies of varying quality. However, they argue that combining many studies helps to average out any differences in climate, soil type, and crop variety.

The debate over whether organic food is better for people has been ongoing for some time. Some experts argue that the benefits of organic food are exaggerated, while others believe that it can provide significant health benefits. The Soil Association, which campaigns for organic farming, says that this research "shatters the myth" that how we farm does not affect the quality of our food.

Emmanuel Limal, a 43-year-old actor from France living in Copenhagen, was tired of dating women who didn't want to start a family. He had been looking for love for 20 years and wanted children. After trying online dating, he became frustrated with people's profiles that focused on hobbies and travel, but not having kids.

Limal has a six-year-old daughter from a previous relationship, but he wants more children. Coming from a big family, he always thought he would have many kids too. However, he struggled to meet someone who shared his desire for a family. He felt it was a taboo topic in dating.

One day, Limal read a profile of a 38-year-old woman who admitted she wanted children. This inspired him to create a dating site called Babyklar.nu, which translates to "baby-ready now." The site is like other dating sites, but with one key difference: users must be honest about wanting to start a family soon.

Limal invested in the site by remortgaging his apartment. He asks users if they are okay with someone who already has children and wants more. However, he doesn't ask them to specify how many kids they want.

The response to the site has been overwhelming. Many people signed up when it launched in June, and some couples have already met through the site and started relationships. Limal expects the first "Babyklar.nu baby" to be born next summer. More men than women have joined the site (53% to 47%), with many saying they feel relieved to be honest about their desire for children.

Scientists have started mapping the bacteria in a city's subway system for the first time. Dr Christopher Mason led a team that swabbed the New York City subway system for 18 months. They found many types of bacteria, including some that can cause illnesses like meningitis, anthrax, and bubonic plague.

However, the team says these findings are not a cause for concern. The amounts of plague and anthrax were very small, and it's likely that rats carried the plague bacteria. No one has fallen ill with plague in New York for years.

Most of the bacteria found are harmless or even beneficial. They help break down toxic waste and process food, just like the bacteria inside our bodies do. Some bacteria reflect the eating habits of different neighborhoods. For example, bacteria associated with cheese were found all over the subway, while those used to make kimchi were more common in certain areas.

The team also found bacteria that can cause illnesses like diarrhea and skin infections. However, these are not spreading disease throughout the city. Instead, they seem to be a normal part of the city's ecosystem.

The researchers collected over 1,000 samples from all 466 open subway stations in New York. They identified 15,152 distinct species, nearly half of which were bacteria. The good news is that these bacteria are not making people sick. In fact, they may even be essential for a healthy city.

Dr Mason says people should not worry about getting infections from the subway. Instead, they should focus on washing their hands and taking care of themselves. He feels more confident riding the subway after this study.

Nelson Mandela, a hero to millions around the world, has died at the age of 95. He was South Africa's first black president and a key figure in the country's fight for freedom.

Mandela passed away at his home in Johannesburg, surrounded by his family. His health had been declining for years, causing him to withdraw from public life. The news was announced by current President Jacob Zuma, who said Mandela had died peacefully around 8:50 pm local time.

Zuma described Mandela as the country's "greatest son" and said he would be remembered for bringing people together. He announced that Mandela would receive a state funeral and ordered flags to fly at half-mast.

World leaders paid tribute to Mandela, including US President Barack Obama, who referred to him by his clan name, Madiba. Obama said Mandela had transformed South Africa through his dignity and willingness to sacrifice his freedom for others.

UK Prime Minister David Cameron described Mandela as "a hero of our time," while FW de Klerk, the former president who freed Mandela from prison, said he was a great unifier who lived reconciliation.

People gathered in the streets of South Africa to celebrate Mandela's life. In Soweto, they sang and danced near his old home, waving South African flags and wearing the colors of his party, the African National Congress (ANC).

Mandela's death has sent South Africa into mourning, nearly 20 years after he led the country from apartheid to democracy. He will also be remembered around the world as a great statesman and moral leader.

Born in 1918, Mandela joined the ANC in 1943 and became a key figure in the fight against apartheid. He was arrested and sentenced to life

More than 100,000 people protested across Brazil against poor public services, high costs for the World Cup, and heavy-handed policing. The protests started peacefully but turned violent in some cities, with clashes between police and protesters, arson attacks on cars and buses, and injuries to several police officers.

The demonstrations took place in many cities, including Rio de Janeiro, São Paulo, Brasilia, Belem, Belo Horizonte, Salvador, and Porto Alegre. Protesters were frustrated with the government's spending on international sporting events while neglecting public services like healthcare and education.

In Rio, a large crowd set fires outside the legislative assembly, smashed windows, and painted graffiti on the walls. Police responded with pepper spray, injuring some protesters. In Brasilia, demonstrators broke through police lines to enter the national congress building. In Belo Horizonte, police clashed with protesters trying to break through a cordon around a football stadium.

The protests were sparked by smaller demonstrations against bus price increases, which led to complaints of excessive police force. The Confederations Cup, a World Cup test event, was also a focus of the protests due to concerns about the costs and quality of public services.

Protesters came from various backgrounds and had different reasons for participating. Some were frustrated with the government's lack of action on issues like education and unemployment. Others were angry about police violence and corruption.

The use of social media played a significant role in spreading the message about the protests, with some protesters carrying banners declaring "We come from Facebook." Many protesters were young and had never participated in such large-scale demonstrations before.

Comparisons have been drawn between Brazil's protests and those in Turkey and other countries. Some protesters wore Guy Fawkes masks

Amsterdam's liberal image may be under threat due to plans to move troublesome neighbours to special villages made from shipping containers. The city's Mayor, Eberhard van der Laan, claims this policy will protect victims of abuse and harassment. However, critics have labelled these villages "scum villages" because they resemble proposals by far-right politician Geert Wilders.

The Mayor's spokesman, Bartho Boer, denies that the plans are intolerant. He says the goal is to defend Amsterdam's liberal values and protect people who are victims of violence and harassment. The villages are not for ordinary neighbour disputes, but for those who are extremely violent and intimidating.

People who cause serious problems will be evicted and moved to basic temporary homes made from shipping containers in industrial areas. These units have showers and kitchens, but are not luxurious. This is intentional, as the city does not want to "reward" these tenants with better accommodation.

The idea of moving troublemakers to special villages has been tried before in the Netherlands, but it led to slums. Boer claims that this time will be different, as the administration has learned from past mistakes and will not house antisocial people together.

In reality, the plan is to scatter individual "scum houses" around the city, rather than creating entire villages. After up to six months in these houses, tenants will be found permanent homes. The city expects to move about ten families a year into this programme, which starts in 2013.

The temporary dwellings will have a strong police presence, but antisocial tenants will also have access to doctors, social workers, and parole officers. This is intended to prevent the same problems from happening again when they are moved to their new homes.

Male bosses in the UK receive bonuses that are nearly double those of their female colleagues doing the same job. This means men get an extra £141,500 over a lifetime compared to women.

According to figures from the Chartered Management Institute (CMI), male managers earned average bonuses of £6,442 in 2012, while women received £3,029. In top roles, female directors got bonuses of £36,270, compared to £63,700 for male directors.

These findings have led to calls for action from equality campaigners. Ann Francke, CMI's chief executive, said: "It's time to make this issue a priority in management. We need to change our approach to allow more flexibility and transparency around performance and rewards."

Dr Ruth Sealy, a researcher at Cranfield School of Management, added: "Bonuses can be given out unfairly. To solve this problem, we need to make bonuses more transparent."

While some data may be skewed by factors such as women entering jobs with fewer bonus payments, the pay gap in Britain remains significant. Full-time male employees earn 10% more than women.

Maria Miller, Minister for Women and Equalities, said: "These figures show that women still lose out to men at work. The government is working to close the pay gap by making pay secrecy clauses illegal and encouraging companies to improve their treatment of women."

Some large companies have signed up to a scheme called Think, Act, Report, which aims to promote equality in the workplace. However, despite some progress, male managers' earnings are rising faster than those of female managers.

Maria sits in a community centre on a cold Tuesday afternoon, waiting for her number to be called. She is number 34. When it's her turn, Maria picks up a bag with essentials like pasta, eggs, and cornflakes, and chooses between butternut squash or carrots as this week's vegetables.

The East Hampton Food Pantry expects over 400 families to collect their weekly food parcel by the end of the day. This pantry is just streets away from some of the most expensive properties in the world. In the summer, the Hamptons are a popular destination for billionaires, but when they leave after Labor Day, the reality of life for the local community sets in.

Maria works 14-hour days cleaning mansions in the summer, but has no work during the winter months. She laughs when asked if she has enough money: "There is no work in the winter, only in the summertime." Many workers in the Hamptons are from Latin America and struggle to make ends meet.

Some families with up to five children live in cramped basements and pay over $1,000 a month in rent. Maria's friends often can't afford heating or medication, and would go hungry without the food pantry. Vicki Littman, chairperson of the East Hampton Food Pantry, says the number of people seeking help is increasing.

Littman explains that outsiders often don't realize there are people struggling to get by in a place known for its wealth. The town has lost key workers like teachers and police officers because they can't afford to live there. Housing is the biggest cost in the Hamptons, with homes selling for millions of dollars.

Robert Mysłajek stops suddenly on a muddy mountain track in Poland. He has found what he was looking for - wolf droppings. Wolf sightings are rare, so finding their faeces is exciting, even for an experienced tracker like him.

There are now around 1,500 wolves in Poland, double the number from 15 years ago. Wolves are one of Europe's last large predator carnivores, along with brown bears, lynxes, and wolverines. Conservationists from Britain, Germany, and the Netherlands come to Poland to learn how the country has protected this species.

Mysłajek, a biologist from the University of Warsaw, examines the droppings carefully. "This wolf ate a red deer," he says. "With DNA tests, I can tell you about its diet, gender, age, health, and family connections."

Polish wolves are known to travel long distances. One wolf even reached the Netherlands, where it was unfortunately hit by a car. They need space, with an average territory of 250 square kilometers per pack.

A group of British students on a field trip to Poland ask Mysłajek about reintroducing wolves to Scotland. The last time wolves were in Scotland was in the 18th century. Mysłajek thinks it's possible but notes that there are differences between Scotland and Poland, such as the type of livestock.

In Poland, wolves help control the population of wild boar, which damage farmers' crops. Wolves are also part of a balanced ecosystem, keeping herbivores in check and allowing trees to grow tall for birds to nest in.

England fan Anthony McDowell from Liverpool walked along Rio's Copacabana beach, enjoying the sunshine before watching a World Cup match. He said, "The place is lovely. The people are great. There's a party atmosphere." However, he wished the England team could be better.

McDowell and his friends were among many supporters who turned the beachfront into a party zone with national colours and chants. Some danced, took photos, or drank while waiting for the next game to start on the big screen. The last time so many people gathered here during the day was when the pope visited.

The cheerful mood was different from the protests, transport chaos, and stadium problems that happened before the World Cup. But now that the football has started, visiting supporters want to enjoy themselves. Brian Hill, a retired chief executive from Sunderland, said, "If I had known how complicated and costly it would be, I wouldn't have come. But now that we're here, it's great."

Hill travelled for over 20 hours to get to Rio and then faced long delays on the road from the airport. His son Andrew had his sunglasses stolen on the beach. They were also surprised that many bars didn't have big screens for the games. However, they loved the atmosphere, even if the logistics were not perfect.

The World Cup has started spectacularly with exciting matches, including Robin van Persie's amazing diving header for the Netherlands against Spain. There have been 28 goals in the first eight games, almost three times as many as at the same stage in South Africa in 2010. Latin-American teams won all their games until now, adding to the carnival mood.

A baby girl born today in the UK can expect to live until she is almost 82 years old on average, while a boy will live until he is 78. In some countries like Andorra, people live even longer - up to 85 and 79 years respectively. However, in other countries like the Central African Republic, life expectancy is much lower, at just 49 and 44 years.

Despite these differences, one thing is clear: almost everywhere in the world, people are living longer. This is especially true for young children, who are now less likely to die than they were 40 years ago. In fact, deaths among under-fives have dropped by nearly 60% since 1970, from 16.4 million to 6.8 million.

To understand these changes and how to improve healthcare, the Institute of Health Metrics and Evaluation (IHME) in Seattle has led a massive project involving almost 500 researchers over five years. They have collected data on the global burden of disease, including how many children die and from what causes. This information will help organizations and governments focus their efforts and resources on keeping people alive.

The IHME's research has produced some surprising results. For example, they found that malaria kills twice as many people each year as previously thought - 1.2 million. Most of these deaths are among adults, not children under five as was commonly believed. This challenges the conventional wisdom that adults become semi-immune to malaria.

The World Health Organization (WHO) has welcomed the IHME's study, but some staff members have expressed caution about the findings. They want to carefully assess the validity of the data before accepting it.

In Rjukan's market square stands a statue of Sam Eyde, the town's founder. He was a famous Norwegian engineer who built the town in the early 1900s to house workers for his factories. Behind him rises the steep Gaustatoppen mountain, and in front of him is another almost vertical mountainside.

Eyde used the power of the Rjukanfossen waterfall to create hydroelectricity at what was then the world's largest power plant. However, he couldn't change the fact that the town lies in shadow for half the year due to its location between high mountains. From late September to mid-March, the town is not completely dark but lacks sunlight.

Recently, three large solar-powered mirrors were installed on the mountain opposite the square. These mirrors track the sun's movement and reflect its rays onto the square, bathing it in bright sunlight. The townspeople are delighted with this new development.

Ingrid Sparbo, a retired secretary who has lived in Rjukan all her life, says that people get used to living in shade but that the new sunlight is "mentally warming." Many residents and visitors enjoy standing in the sun, taking photographs, and smiling at its warmth. Some are more cautious, like electrical engineer Eivind Toreid, who notes that it's not real sunlight but feels like a spotlight.

The man behind this project is Martin Andersen, an artist who moved to Rjukan in 2001. He was inspired by the lack of sunlight during his daily walks with his child and wanted to create something to bring happiness to the town. After 12 years, his idea became a reality when a German company installed the mirrors.

Dr. Izumi Tabata's training method sounds too good to be true - just four minutes a day to get fit. But when you try it, you realize how wrong you were. The method involves 20 seconds of all-out effort, followed by 10 seconds of rest, repeated eight times.

Tabata first tried this method on his university students in the early 1990s. They were exhausted after just four minutes, but after six weeks, they saw surprising results. Tabata's research was inspired by Japan's speed skating team, who used short bursts of intense exercise to improve their performance.

To test his theory, Tabata divided a group of moderately trained students into two groups. One group did an hour of steady cardiovascular exercise on a stationary bike five times a week. The other group did a 10-minute warm-up, followed by four minutes of Tabata intervals, four times a week, plus one longer session.

The results were impressive. After six weeks, the group doing Tabata's method had improved their anaerobic capacity by 28% and their cardiovascular health by 15%. The control group, who trained for five hours a week, also improved their cardiovascular health, but only by 10%.

Tabata's method is not easy. You need to give it your all - 170% of your maximum effort. If you feel okay afterwards, you're not doing it right. The first few repetitions might feel easy, but the last ones will be extremely hard.

Some people think that only experienced athletes can do Tabata's method, but Tabata disagrees. He says that anyone can do it, as long as they start with a trainer who can help them find the right intensity.

In 2005, BlackBerry introduced instant messaging on mobile phones, which helped the company become very successful. At that time, the iPhone didn't exist yet, and BlackBerry's innovations made its smartphone one of Canada's top exports.

Six years later, in 2011, riots broke out in London and other UK cities. BlackBerry Messenger (BBM) was so effective at organizing the rioters that politicians wanted to shut it down temporarily. However, two years later, users themselves are abandoning BBM. As demand for BlackBerry phones decreases, dozens of alternative messaging apps have appeared, including Facebook's and Apple's own apps, as well as independent services like WhatsApp and Kik.

These new apps offer free downloads and use the internet to send text messages, pictures, voice clips, stickers, and videos between different types of phones. To stay competitive, BBM has been released on Android and Apple devices, with over 20 million downloads announced. Despite this initial interest, many believe that BBM's wider release won't save the service.

BBM claims to have 80 million monthly users after its upgrade, but WhatsApp has 300 million. Other services offer features that BBM lacks, such as video or voice calls, location sharing, and sticker options. Even basic features like contacts and calendar sharing are not available on Apple and Android versions of BBM.

The way people message is changing from text-based to visual. Photos shared on Instagram spark conversations, and Snapchat's self-deleting pictures have opened up new possibilities. All these services are free for any phone with an internet connection.

A big argument has started between countries about whether indigenous people in Bolivia should be allowed to chew coca leaves. Coca leaves are the main ingredient in cocaine. Bolivia has been given special permission from the 1961 Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs, which sets international rules on drugs, to let its indigenous people chew the leaves.

Bolivia argued that this convention went against its new constitution, adopted in 2009, which says it must protect coca as part of its cultural heritage. The constitution also states that coca is not a narcotic in its natural state. For centuries, South American Indians have been chewing coca leaves for energy and medicinal purposes.

Supporters of Bolivia's position praised the country for standing up for indigenous people's rights. "Bolivia's move is inspiring and groundbreaking," said Danny Kushlick from the Transform Drug Policy Foundation. "It shows that any country can change its engagement with UN conventions if it wants to."

However, the UN's International Narcotics Control Board (INCB) has accused Bolivia of threatening international drug control rules. Several countries, including the UK, US, Italy, Sweden, Netherlands, and Russia, opposed Bolivia's demands.

The UK expressed concerns that allowing coca leaf chewing could lead to more coca production and cocaine trafficking. "This would weaken international law on tackling the drugs trade," it said.

In 1964, when Bolivia was under a dictatorship, it signed up to the convention, which banned coca leaf chewing. However, Bolivia was given 25 years to implement this ban, which expired in 1989. Since then, the issue has been disputed.

In 1996, Carl Sagan recorded a message for future Mars explorers, saying: "I'm glad you're on Mars, and I wish I was with you." Seventeen years later, a Dutch company called Mars One wants to make Sagan's dream of reaching Mars a reality. They plan to send four astronauts to the Red Planet in 2023 to set up a human colony.

However, there are two major problems. Firstly, the gravity on Mars is only 38% of Earth's, which would cause big changes in the astronauts' bodies. This means they might not be able to survive if they returned to Earth. Secondly, because of this problem, the astronauts will have to say goodbye to their families and friends forever, as there won't be a return ticket.

The Mars One website explains that returning from Mars is extremely difficult. It would require a powerful rocket, life support systems for up to seven months, and a way to safely land back on Earth. Despite these challenges, over 10,000 people have applied to join the mission, including men and women aged between 18 and 62.

One applicant, an American woman named Cynthia, was inspired by Carl Sagan when she met him as a child. She told Mars One that she wants to be one of the pioneers on Mars and show people that there are still new frontiers to explore.

Mars One is looking for astronauts who are resilient, adaptable, curious, trustworthy, and resourceful. The company's founder, Bas Lansdorp, believes that the mission is feasible using existing technology. He says that the basic elements needed for life, such as water and air, are already present on Mars.

A team from Leicester University has announced that they have found the body of Richard III, the last king of the Plantagenet family. The discovery was made in a car park in Leicester, where the church of Grey Friars once stood. The team is "beyond reasonable doubt" that the body is Richard's.

The announcement was made at a press conference, where scientists and historians shared their findings. They used DNA tests, computer imaging, and historical records to identify the body. A descendant of Richard's sister was found to have matching DNA, which helped confirm the identity.

Richard III died in battle on August 22, 1485, at Bosworth Field. The researchers showed how he was killed by a blow to the head from a halberd, a medieval battle weapon. He would have been unconscious immediately and dead soon after. Other injuries were inflicted after his death, suggesting that his body was mistreated.

The team also found evidence of a gruesome ritual on the battlefield and as Richard's body was brought back to Leicester. His naked corpse was likely carried on horseback, mocked and abused along the way. One injury, a stab wound to the buttock, could only have happened after death, when his lower body was no longer protected by armor.

A new tomb is being designed for Richard III in Leicester Cathedral, near the excavation site. A ceremony will be held next year to lay him to rest. The city's museums are also planning a new visitor center to showcase the discovery.

The discovery has been met with excitement and shock. Michael Ibsen, the descendant of Richard's sister, said he was still trying to process the news. "He was a king, but just one of the dead," he said.

Scientists have successfully implanted a false memory in mice's brains. This experiment aims to understand why people sometimes remember events that never happened. False memories can lead to wrongful convictions, as eyewitness testimony is not always reliable.

To study this phenomenon, Susumu Tonagawa and his team at MIT manipulated individual brain cells in mice to create false memories. They used a technique called optogenetics, which allows for precise control over brain cells. The researchers engineered brain cells in the hippocampus, a region involved in forming memories, to produce a protein that responds to blue light.

In the experiment, mice were placed in a chamber and allowed to explore it. The next day, they were given an electric shock in a different chamber while their memory of the first chamber was activated using light. As a result, the mice associated fear with the first chamber, even though they had never been shocked there.

Tonagawa believes that a similar process might occur in humans when powerful false memories are created. "Humans are imaginative animals," he said. "We can associate what's happening in our minds with external events, creating false associations."

The study showed that false and genuine memories rely on similar brain mechanisms, making it difficult to distinguish between them. Tonagawa hopes that this research will alert lawmakers and legal experts to the unreliability of memory.

Chris French, a leading researcher in false memories, said that these results are an important first step in understanding their neural basis. However, he noted that the false memories created in mice were simpler than those experienced by humans, such as false memories of childhood trauma or alien abduction.

Mark Stokes, a neuroscientist at Oxford University, praised the experiment but emphasized that it's still far from most people's idea of memory.

Music subscription services such as Spotify and Deezer are now making over $1 billion in sales worldwide. More people are choosing to pay for music online, which has led to a 50% increase in streaming and subscription revenues in 2013. This growth helped overall music sales in Europe rise for the first time in 12 years.

There are around 450 music rental services globally, and many people still listen to music for free. However, more music fans are willing to pay for these services because they offer a wide range of choices. The number of paying subscribers has increased from 8 million to 28 million over three years.

These subscription services are easily accessible on smartphones and tablets, making them popular among people who want to try new music without buying it. Consumers like that these services are affordable, easy to use, and legal alternatives to pirated downloads. The head of the International Federation of the Phonographic Industry (IFPI), Frances Moore, said that "music streaming and subscription is now a mainstream model for our business."

In some countries, such as Britain and America, streaming may soon generate more revenue than music downloads from online stores like Apple's iTunes. Subscription services currently account for one-third of all digital sales globally.

The IFPI found that the number of people using subscription and streaming services increased in several countries. In the US, this percentage rose from 19% to 23%, while in Britain it grew from 19% to 22%. However, the number of downloaders remained steady or decreased slightly.

A thick layer of bird droppings covers the golden railings of one of Britain's most expensive houses, The Towers. Pigeon skeletons lie among broken mirrors and water flows through damaged decorations. This £30m palace is on "Billionaires' Row" in north London, but it has been left to ruin.

The Bishops Avenue, where The Towers is located, is a street in the heart of London's expensive property market. Ten mansions here have stood almost empty for 25 years, believed to be owned by members of the Saudi Arabian royal family. Their grand columns are cracking and their swimming pools are filled with rubble. Nature has taken over, with owls even moving in.

This scene is repeated along the avenue, which Lloyds Bank says is the second most expensive street in Britain. While many people struggle to buy a house in London, 16 mansions on this street sit empty, often behind locked gates and with steel grilles covering their windows. Guard dogs patrol the overgrown grounds.

Across the street stands another derelict mansion worth £18m, with smashed windows and anti-climb paint on its walls. Another mansion, sold for £20m, has metal grilles blocking its windows.

Despite this, house prices continue to rise. One mansion, Dryades, was sold for £12m in 2007 but is now believed to be worth £30m. Heath Lodge, where a fashion tycoon was murdered in 1984, is now worth £13m after being sold for £400,000 in the late 1970s.

The neglect of these properties can be frustrating for people struggling to find a place to live in one of the world's most expensive cities.

To Tua Pittman, a master navigator from Raratonga in the Cook Islands, a canoe is more than just a way to travel. "A canoe is like our island, and the crew members are like our community," he says. He believes that navigating a canoe is not just about using the stars, moon, sun, and birds to get from one place to another. It's also about being a leader and showing your crew the right way.

Tua and his team sailed over 6,000 nautical miles (11,000 km) in traditional canoes to reach Sydney for the World Parks Congress. They started their journey on September 25th in the Cook Islands and traveled through Samoa, Fiji, Vanuatu, and the Gold Coast before arriving in Sydney. Around 100 crew members were involved in different parts of the trip. Unfortunately, they had to use modern navigation equipment sometimes because traditional methods weren't enough.

The Mua Voyage was a partnership between the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) and five Pacific Island countries: Samoa, Tonga, New Zealand, the Cook Islands, and Fiji. The main goal was to deliver an important message to the World Parks Congress. The message said that the ocean is being overused and damaged. Fish and other sea creatures are disappearing, and coral reefs are dying.

The message also talked about how foreign fishing fleets are taking too many resources from Pacific Island waters. The crew members were worried because they saw these changes happening during their journey. They wanted to tell the world that something needs to be done to protect the ocean.

Dame Sally Davies, England's Chief Medical Officer, has compared the problem of antibiotic resistance to the threat of international terrorism. This comparison may seem extreme, but the reality is even more alarming. Every year, many more people die from bacterial infections that are resistant to antibiotics than from terrorist attacks.

The World Health Organization estimates that multi-drug resistant tuberculosis alone causes over 150,000 deaths annually. Antibiotic resistance is no longer a distant threat; it's a harsh reality. In the past century, our life expectancy has increased dramatically due to advances in public health, vaccination, and antibiotics. A child born in Britain today has a good chance of living to be 100 years old.

However, this progress is under threat. The overuse and misuse of antibiotics have led to the emergence of resistant bacteria. In hospitals, where powerful antibiotics are used frequently, these resistant organisms thrive. As a doctor, I've seen the rise of Methicillin Resistant Staphylococcus Aureus (MRSA) and other resistant species.

We've become complacent about our ability to control infectious diseases with antibiotics. But the balance is shifting. The pharmaceutical industry is not developing new antibiotics quickly enough to keep up with the evolving resistance. New, more resistant species have emerged, and even last-line drugs like vancomycin are no longer effective against some bacteria.

The development of new antibiotics has become increasingly difficult and expensive. As a result, pharmaceutical companies are less inclined to invest in this area. The first signs of antibiotic resistance appeared soon after their widespread use began in the 1940s. Initially, these cases were rare, but now they're common.

In the southern town of Butare, Rwanda, people from all over the country and neighboring Burundi come to visit a small shop called Inzozi Nziza, which means "Sweet Dreams". They want to try something new - ice cream. At this ice cream parlour, customers can buy scoops in different flavors like sweet cream, passion fruit, strawberry, and pineapple. They can also add fresh fruit, honey, chocolate chips, or granola on top. The shop sells black tea and coffee too.

The manager, Louise Ingabire, says that the shop is "changing lives" by introducing people to ice cream. She believes that ice cream is important because it's something new for many Rwandans. Some people like it, but others need to be convinced that they'll enjoy it.

For Ingabire, working at Inzozi Nziza has made a big difference in her life. Before, she didn't have a job and stayed at home. Now, she has a vision for the future and can earn money to support her family.

The shop is popular among students from the National University of Rwanda, who come to treat themselves to something cool and different. A student named Kalisa Migendo says that Inzozi Nziza brings people together. "If you want to meet a friend or go on a date, you come here for an ice cream," he says.

Most of the ingredients used in the shop are sourced locally, except for vanilla beans and cocoa, which are imported. The milk comes from a nearby depot.

More than one-third of all women worldwide will experience physical or sexual violence at some point in their lives. This is usually committed by a male partner, according to a comprehensive study by the World Health Organization (WHO). The report reveals that 30% of women are attacked by their partners, and 38% of murders of women are carried out by intimate partners.

The WHO's director general, Dr Margaret Chan, said these findings show that violence against women is a major global health problem. "Health systems can and must do more to help women who experience violence," she added.

Africa has the highest levels of violence against women, with nearly half (45.6%) experiencing physical or sexual violence. In low- and middle-income Europe, 27.2% of women will suffer violence. However, even in wealthy countries, a third of women (32.7%) will experience violence at some point.

The report found that 42% of women who suffer violence sustain injuries, which can lead to them seeking medical help. This is often the first opportunity for healthcare staff to detect domestic violence and offer support. Violence has a significant impact on women's health, causing broken bones, pregnancy complications, and mental illness.

Two reports from the WHO provide data on the prevalence of violence against women and guidelines for healthcare staff on how to help them. The reports were written by Dr Claudia Garcia-Moreno and Professor Charlotte Watts, who specialize in gender, violence, and health.

The researchers compared data from around the world and found that partner violence and sexual violence have a significant impact on women's health, including increasing the risk of HIV, depression, and unwanted pregnancies. They also found that better-educated women and those with jobs are less likely to suffer violence

A highly valuable artwork by the artist Banksy was about to be sold at an auction in Florida, but the sale was suddenly stopped just before it began. 
The artwork, called "Slave Labour", shows a child making flags and is seen as a commentary on social issues. It was expected to sell for around $700,000. 
However, the owner of the auction house, Frederic Thut, announced that the piece would not be sold after all. He did not give a reason, but community leaders in London were very happy with the decision. 

The artwork had been removed from a wall in north London without permission and was being sold by an unknown person through the auction house. 
Community leaders had campaigned to stop the sale and were pleased that their efforts had paid off. "We're halfway there," said Alan Strickland, a local councillor. "One of our demands was that it doesn't sell, and now we want it back." 

The leader of Haringey Council, Claire Kober, had written to the Arts Council England and the Mayor of Miami to ask them to intervene and stop the sale. 
However, it seems that the decision to withdraw the artwork came from the auction house owners after consulting with their lawyers. The FBI would not confirm whether they were investigating the matter.

The auction house later released a statement saying that they had persuaded the owners of the two Banksy artworks to pull them from the sale. 
About 30 potential buyers attended the auction, which continued without the two Banksy pieces. Critics have accused the auction house of selling stolen property, but Thut insisted that the seller was the rightful owner and that the sale was legal.

A significant day at Liverpool's Anglican Cathedral marked a major milestone for the families of the 96 people who lost their lives unnecessarily at Hillsborough football ground. The phrase "the truth" was repeated throughout the day, as it was the same phrase infamously misused by The Sun newspaper in a headline that spread false stories about the disaster.

Margaret Aspinall, whose 18-year-old son James died in the tragedy, said that the families had been fighting for 23 years to uncover the truth. Aspinall, Chair of the Hillsborough Family Support Group, welcomed the apology given by David Cameron for the government's failings in the disaster.

The Hillsborough Independent Panel reviewed 450,000 documents and produced a 395-page report that exposed official mistakes and cleared the names of the victims and football supporters. The report revealed that the police had deliberately tried to shift the blame onto the supporters, claiming they were drunk or didn't have tickets. However, there was no evidence to support these claims.

The panel found that the police had tested the blood of the victims for alcohol levels, which was an unusual decision with no clear reason. They also checked if the victims had a criminal record. The report concluded that there was no evidence of exceptional drunkenness or violence among Liverpool fans.

The Chief Constable at the time, Peter Wright, met with his police federation just four days after the disaster to prepare a defense and create a false story about the events. This meeting took place on the same day that The Sun published its headline "The Truth" over lies fed by senior South Yorkshire police officers.

The panel's report supported allegations that senior police officers had altered junior officers' statements to remove criticism of the police and emphasize misbehavior

Facebook's user numbers are falling in its biggest markets, according to independent data. This is happening as people look for new social networks to use. Facebook will soon report on how it did financially in the first three months of the year. Analysts think it made 36% more money than last year.

However, studies show that Facebook's growth in the US, UK, and other major European countries has stopped. In the past month, Facebook lost 6 million users in the US (a 4% fall) and 1.4 million users in the UK (a 4.5% fall). Over six months, it lost nearly 9 million monthly visitors in the US and 2 million in the UK.

Users are also leaving Facebook in Canada, Spain, France, Germany, and Japan. A Facebook spokeswoman refused to comment on this. Ian Maude, a new media specialist, said that most people who want to use Facebook already have an account. He added that people get bored with the same old thing and like to try something new.

Other social networks are becoming more popular, especially among younger users. Instagram, which Facebook owns, has seen a big increase in popularity. Path, a mobile phone-based social network, is gaining 1 million users per week. It now has over 9 million users.

Facebook is still growing fast in South America and India. However, in developed markets, user numbers are falling. Analysts at Jefferies bank have created an algorithm that shows Facebook's global user numbers may have fallen from their peak.

Vienna has been named the best city to live in the world, while Baghdad is the worst. London, Paris, and New York did not make it into the top 35 cities.

According to a study by Mercer, German-speaking cities are among the best places to live. Vienna was joined by Zurich, Munich, Dusseldorf, and Frankfurt in the top seven. 

Paris has fallen ten places to 37th due to its vulnerability to terrorist attacks. London is ranked 39th. The study looked at social and economic conditions, health, education, housing, and the environment.

Vienna's high ranking is partly because of its affordable housing. A 100sq-metre apartment in a good area costs around €800 per month. In comparison, a similar apartment in London would cost over £2,000.

US cities did not do well in the study due to concerns about personal safety and crime. San Francisco was the highest-ranking US city at 28th, while Boston was 34th. Canadian cities, such as Vancouver, ranked higher than their US counterparts.

Vienna's safe environment, good public transport, and geographical location make it an attractive place to live. The city has a strong economy, with one of the highest GDP per head in the world.

Zurich was named as having the second-highest quality of life, but Vienna is considered more fun due to its young and lively atmosphere. The city is becoming increasingly popular with tourists, with 588,000 British visitors in 2015.

The European migrant crisis has had little impact on Vienna, which has accommodated 90,000 refugees. London's poor scores for air pollution, traffic congestion, and climate have kept it out of the top ten

The Moroccan city of Ouarzazate is no stranger to big productions. Located on the edge of the Sahara Desert, it has hosted many famous films and TV shows, including Lawrence of Arabia, The Mummy, and Game of Thrones. Now, the city is home to a new blockbuster project - a massive solar power plant that will help Morocco become a global leader in renewable energy.

The plant, called Noor, is made up of four linked solar mega-plants that will provide nearly half of Morocco's electricity from renewables by 2020. The project is a key part of Morocco's plan to use its desert sun to generate clean energy and reduce its reliance on imported fossil fuels. When complete, the Noor plant will be the largest concentrated solar power plant in the world.

The first phase of the project, called Noor 1, is set to go live in November 2015. It uses a unique mirror technology that can continue producing power even after the sun goes down. The mirrors are arranged in rows and follow the sun as it moves across the sky, generating heat that is used to produce steam and drive turbines.

Morocco's Environment Minister, Hakima el-Haite, believes that solar energy could have a huge impact on the region, just like oil production did in the past. But for now, the focus is on using solar power to meet Morocco's own energy needs. The country currently imports 94% of its energy as fossil fuels from abroad, which has a big impact on its budget.

Sweden's prisons have a reputation for being progressive. But are they too soft? In 2013, the head of Sweden's prison service, Nils Oberg, announced that four prisons would be closed due to a surprising drop in prisoner numbers.

Between 2011 and 2012, the number of prisoners in Sweden fell by 6%, from around 4,800 to 4,500. This decrease was not because crime rates had fallen, but rather because fewer people were being sent to prison. Oberg was puzzled by this trend, but hoped that it was due to the efforts made by prisons to help prisoners change their behavior.

Kenneth Gustafsson, governor of Kumla Prison, Sweden's most secure jail, says that the Swedish prison system has changed a lot since he joined in 1978. "When I started, we focused on treating prisoners well," he says. "But after some high-profile escapes in 2004, we had to balance this with security."

Despite this shift towards greater security, Sweden still takes a humane approach to sentencing. Prison sentences are generally short, and those who receive life imprisonment can apply for their sentence to be reduced after ten years.

Sweden was the first country in Europe to use electronic tags on prisoners, and it tries to avoid short prison sentences whenever possible. Instead, it uses community-based measures that have been shown to reduce reoffending. As a result, Sweden's reoffending rate is relatively low, at around 30-40% over three years.

The traditional eight-hour workday is coming to an end for many Japanese workers. However, leaving the office on time and having dinner at home can be seen as disloyal by some employers. 

For decades, companies in Japan have pushed their employees to work long hours without taking enough breaks. But now, the government wants to change this culture of overwork. They are considering a law that would require workers to take at least five days of paid holiday per year.

Currently, Japanese employees are entitled to an average of 18.5 days of paid holiday per year, but most don't use all their days off. In fact, they typically only take nine days off out of the 18.5 days they're allowed. This is very different from workers in other countries like Britain and France, who usually take more time off.

The government hopes that this new law will encourage Japanese employees to take more breaks and follow the example of workers in other countries. Japan's work culture has contributed to its economic success, but it has also led to problems such as a low birth rate and high levels of stress-related illnesses.

Many Japanese employees work long hours, with about 22% working more than 49 hours per week. This is much higher than in countries like the US, France, and Germany. Some workers even die from overwork, known as "karoshi," with around 200 cases reported each year.

The government wants to change this culture of overwork and encourage employees to take time off to rest and recharge. However, many workers are afraid to take breaks because they don't want to be seen as lazy or disloyal by their employers.

British author David Mitchell has written a novel that won't be read for 100 years. The book is part of the Future Library project, created by Scottish artist Katie Paterson. In 2014, 1,000 trees were planted in Oslo's Nordmarka forest. Each year, an author will write a piece of work that will only be printed on paper made from these trees in 2114.

Mitchell is the second writer to contribute to the project, after Margaret Atwood. He wrote his manuscript, called From Me Flows What You Call Time, and handed it over in a ceremony in the forest. The title comes from a piece of music by Japanese composer Toru Takemitsu, but Mitchell won't say what the book is about.

The Future Library project gives authors a unique chance to write without worrying about criticism or praise. Mitchell said that not being able to see how people react to his work was "liberating." He usually spends a lot of time editing his writing, but this time he had to finish quickly and didn't have time to make changes.

The project's creator, Katie Paterson, asked writers to explore the theme of imagination and time. Mitchell read a short story and a poem by William Wordsworth during the ceremony in the forest. The trees will be cared for over the next 98 years before they are used to print the manuscripts.

Mitchell said that it's hard to imagine that his writing will still be interesting to people in 100 years. But he likes the idea of creating something that will outlast him. His manuscript is now sealed and stored alongside Atwood's in a special room in Oslo's new public library, where it will remain until it's printed in 211

An octopus named Inky has escaped from the National Aquarium in New Zealand. He broke out of his tank and slid down a 50-metre drainpipe into the sea. This happened after the lid of his tank was left slightly open by mistake.

Inky, a common New Zealand octopus, made his escape at night when no one was around. Staff think he climbed to the top of his tank, then went across the floor and down the drainpipe. The pipe led directly to the sea on the east coast of New Zealand's North Island.

Rob Yarrell, manager of the aquarium, said: "Octopuses are famous for escaping. I don't think Inky was unhappy or lonely. He's just a curious octopus who wants to know what's happening outside." 

Inky might have slid across the floor and then into the drainpipe. Another possibility is that he squeezed into an open pipe at the top of his tank, which led under the floor to the drain.

When staff found Inky's empty tank the next morning, they were surprised. Yarrell said: "We're sad, but this is typical of Inky. He's always been a surprise." 

Reiss Jenkinson, an exhibits keeper, is sure that Inky wasn't taken by someone. "I know how octopuses behave," he said. "They can fit into very small spaces and are extremely intelligent."

Octopuses have no bones, so they can squeeze through tiny gaps. They're also known to be clever and use tools. At another aquarium in Wellington, an octopus was found stealing crabs from another tank at night.

Why do referees put themselves through the stress and criticism that comes with their job? Talking to some of the top young referees in England, it's clear they have thought about this question a lot. This season, there has been a lot of criticism of referees, with some former referees speaking out about the standards.

So why do these young referees want to become part of this profession? Why spend hours driving around the country, making decisions that will inevitably upset some people, and working towards refereeing big games on TV in front of millions of people?

Lee Swabey, a highly-rated young referee, gives us a glimpse into what motivates him. After refereeing a match between Grimsby and Woking, he says he got the best reward possible: "Twenty-two handshakes" from the players, plus praise from both managers. This is what all referees hope for after a game - a sense of satisfaction that everything went smoothly.

Swabey knows he's being watched by the Professional Game Match Officials Limited (PGMOL), who are responsible for developing and supporting referees in England. The PGMOL's chief, Mike Riley, was at his match, along with coach Steve Dunn, who was taking notes on every significant decision Swabey made.

A few weeks earlier, Riley and Dunn watched another young referee, John Brooks, officiate a level-5 match. Brooks hopes to get promoted to the Premier League one day and referee some of the biggest games in England. However, his match was called off due to a frozen pitch, which gave him an opportunity to show how he handles tricky situations.

When you walk into a store, you're being watched. But it's not just to stop shoplifting. New technology is helping retailers learn more about you, like your age, sex, and size. They want to know how you shop so they can show you ads that interest you.

About 30% of retailers use facial recognition technology to track customers in-store. This technology uses cameras to analyze faces and compare them to a database. It can even recognize what clothes you're wearing. But the goal isn't to create a database of individual people, it's to understand general shopping habits.

For example, if a woman with a gold necklace walks into a store, the system might predict she wants to buy socks. The retailer could then show her ads for socks on screens in the store. This is similar to how online retailers use data to target ads at you.

However, bringing this technology into physical stores isn't easy. People react differently to cameras than they do to online tracking cookies. Some companies are using machine learning and artificial intelligence to analyze what people wear, like their shoes, to guess their demographics.

One company, Hoxton Analytics, can identify a person's gender with 75-80% accuracy just by looking at their shoes. The CEO says this approach is less invasive than facial recognition because it doesn't involve pointing a camera at someone's face.

Retailers want to find ways to collect data without being too intrusive. But some people think analyzing what you wear, even if it's just your shoes, is still an invasion of privacy. Others argue that as long as the data isn't personally identifiable, it's not a problem.

Insects are full of protein, easy to find, and might soon be on your plate. For a long time, people in most parts of the world haven't considered them as food, but this is changing. In spring 2013, there will be an effort to make insects more acceptable as food and sell them in supermarkets.

In April, London will host Pestival 2013, a festival that celebrates insects and includes eating them. A famous restaurant team from Scandinavia will run a temporary restaurant serving insect-based dishes. This team works with Noma, a Danish restaurant named the world's best for three years running. Its chef, René Redzepi, says ants taste like lemon and some insects can be used to make sauces.

A BBC documentary in March will show food writer Stefan Gates trying deep-fried locusts and barbecued tarantulas. But behind these unusual foods is a serious message: eating insects could help the environment. Many experts think this because insects are abundant, don't need chemicals, and produce fewer greenhouse gases than traditional livestock.

The United Nations' Food and Agriculture Organization has been supporting projects to promote insect farming in Asia and Africa since 2011. In these regions, about two billion people already eat insects regularly. The organization published a list of nearly 2,000 edible insect species in 2012 and plans an international conference on the topic.

Insects are plentiful – for every person, there are 40 tons of them – so they won't become endangered if we eat them. Chef Redzepi points out that people already eat honey, which is made by bees, and that many foods contain insects without us realizing it. He believes nothing should be considered inedible.

The International Energy Agency (IEA) says that coal may become the world's biggest source of energy within five years, which could have disastrous effects on the climate. One reason for the increase in coal use is the rise of shale gas in the US, which has led to a decrease in coal consumption there. As a result, global coal prices have dropped, making it more attractive to other countries.

The IEA reports that coal consumption is increasing worldwide, except in the US. Even countries with targets to reduce carbon emissions are using more coal. Maria van der Hoeven, Executive Director of the IEA, warns that if policies don't change, coal will catch up with oil as the world's biggest energy source within a decade.

Coal is abundant and cheap to extract, which has led to its widespread use. In the past decade, it met nearly half of the global increase in energy demand. China and India are expected to drive the growth in coal use over the next five years, with India likely to become the world's second-biggest consumer after China.

The IEA predicts that the world will burn 1.2 billion more tonnes of coal per year by 2017, which is equivalent to the current consumption of Russia and the US combined. This increase in coal use will contribute significantly to climate change, as coal produces high levels of carbon emissions when burned.

Van der Hoeven says that a high carbon price is needed to discourage the growth in coal use and encourage cleaner technologies like renewable energy. However, without such a price, only competition from cheaper gas can reduce demand for coal. This has happened in the US, where the increase in shale gas production has led to a decrease in coal use.

Many people know they don't get enough sleep, but what if a simple solution could fix it: sleeping in later? Dr Paul Kelley, from Oxford University's Sleep and Circadian Neuroscience Institute, thinks schools should have different start times to match their students' natural body rhythms. This would improve how well students think, their exam results, and their health. Lack of sleep has been linked to serious problems like diabetes, depression, obesity, and a weakened immune system.

Kelley says that when children are around 10 years old, they naturally wake up at about 6:30 am. But as they get older, this time changes. At 16, it's more like 8 am, and at 18, it's around 9 am. The usual school start time works for younger kids but not for teenagers. For older teens, starting school at 11 am or later might be better.

Kelley says it's not just about telling teenagers to go to bed earlier. Our bodies have a natural rhythm controlled by light, which affects our brain and its internal clock. It's like trying to control your heartbeat - it's not that simple.

Not just students would benefit from a later start time. Kelley thinks the workday should be more flexible to fit people's natural rhythms. He says that most people don't get enough sleep, especially between the ages of 14 and 55. This can affect their mood, performance, and health.

Kelley suggests that workplaces could have different start times for different age groups. For example, older workers could start at 8 am, while younger ones start later. Felix Baumgartner stood at the edge of space above New Mexico's desert. He took a deep breath before jumping from 24 miles high. "Our guardian angel will take care of you," said mission control. Ten minutes later, he landed safely on Earth after reaching speeds of up to 725mph and breaking three world records.

Baumgartner became the first person to break the sound barrier while skydiving, reaching Mach 1.24. He also set records for the highest altitude manned balloon flight and the highest altitude skydive. His team cheered as he raised his arms in victory. Baumgartner wore a special suit that protected him from extreme pressure changes during his jump.

Before jumping, Baumgartner had to wait two days due to bad weather. On Sunday morning, a huge balloon carried him up into clear skies. At the top, he checked 40 items with his mentor Joe Kittinger, who previously held the record for the highest altitude manned balloon flight. There was some concern about a heater in Baumgartner's visor not working, but they decided to proceed.

The jump was watched by a record 8 million people on YouTube. Three cameras attached to Baumgartner's suit recorded his four-minute free-fall and parachute opening. The success of the mission raises hopes that astronauts might be able to survive high-altitude disasters in the future.

Baumgartner has done many daring stunts before, including parachuting off buildings and mountains. He had practiced two free-falls from 71,000 feet and 97,000 feet before this attempt. This jump was seven years in the planning and sponsored by Red Bull drinks.

Barack Obama returned to Washington on Wednesday after winning the presidential election. In his victory speech in Chicago, he called for unity and action from the American people. However, it's unlikely that he will get a smooth start as he faces a Republican-led House of Representatives and a looming budget crisis.

Obama won the election by securing more than 270 electoral college votes and getting a higher share of the popular vote. He beat his opponent Mitt Romney in many key states, including Ohio, Virginia, and Colorado. Despite this, America remains deeply divided.

The President is now looking to establish a lasting legacy in his second term. He wants to focus on economic recovery, immigration reform, education, climate change, and foreign policy issues like Iran and Israel-Palestine. However, he faces opposition from Republicans who want to protect military spending and reject tax increases.

In their statements, Republican House Speaker John Boehner and Democratic Senate Leader Harry Reid called for cooperation to address the country's challenges. Obama has already started negotiations with Boehner, but it remains to be seen how successful they will be.

The stock market reacted negatively to the election result, with shares dropping sharply on the Dow. The new Congress, which will take office in January, is expected to look similar to the current one, with a Republican majority in the House and a slim Democratic majority in the Senate.

In his victory speech, Obama referred to the need for electoral reform and returned to his message of hope from the 2008 election. He told his supporters that America's best days are yet to come and emphasized the importance of unity. Romney conceded graciously, urging politicians to work together to address the country's challenges.

Sweden has been ranked as the best country for older people, while Afghanistan is the worst, according to a new global index on ageing. The Global AgeWatch index shows that being rich does not necessarily mean better conditions for people over 60. 

The US, which is the world's richest country, ranks eighth in the list, and the UK comes in at number 13. Sri Lanka ranks higher than Pakistan, despite having a similar economy. Some countries like Bolivia and Mauritius do well on the index, even though they are not very rich.

Mark Gorman from HelpAge International said: "This survey shows that history is important. The top-ranked countries were not always wealthy, but they made good decisions about pensions and healthcare." He added that all countries face limited resources, but they should remember to address issues of old age when making investment decisions.

The index covers 91 countries and includes data on 89% of the world's older people. It comes at a time when the population is ageing rapidly: by 2050, there will be two billion people aged 60 and over, which is more than a fifth of the world's population.

In developing countries, the population is ageing faster. More than two-thirds of older people live in poor countries, and this proportion is expected to increase to four-fifths by 2050. Some countries like Brazil are ageing very quickly: it will take only 21 years for the number of older people to double, compared to 115 years in France.

The index shows that countries with fast-ageing populations often struggle to support their older citizens. Women generally live longer than men and face more challenges in old age due to lack of paid work, decision-making power, and vulnerability to violence

Clay Cockrell sits in his office near Central Park, where he often holds therapy sessions with some of New York's wealthiest people. As a former Wall Street worker turned therapist, he spends much of his time walking through parks and listening to the concerns of the extremely wealthy.

Cockrell became an expert in wealth therapy naturally, as many of his clients felt that their problems were not taken seriously by other therapists. "The 1% feel guilty about being rich," he says. "They hide their wealth and often feel isolated." This feeling of isolation has worsened since the financial crisis and the debate over income inequality.

Wealth psychologists argue that the media has contributed to this problem by portraying the rich in a negative light. Jamie Traeger-Muney, founder of the Wealth Legacy Group, says that the Occupy Wall Street movement singled out the 1% and made them feel ashamed of their wealth. "People's reactions to you can be scary when you have a lot of money," adds Barbara Nusbaum, an expert in money psychology.

As a result, many wealthy individuals socialize only with others who are also rich, not because they are snobbish but because they want to be around people who understand their problems. The growing gap between the rich and poor is a global issue, with the richest 1% owning more than half of the world's wealth.

In the US, the top 0.1% households have seen their wealth increase from 7% to 22% over the past three decades, while the bottom 90% have seen their wealth decline. The number of extremely wealthy people has also risen, with 10.1 million households now having $1 million or more in assets.

Takahito Iguchi thinks Google Glasses are not cool. He has a point - there's already a website showing people wearing them looking silly or smug. Iguchi, a Japanese entrepreneur, hopes to do better with his own augmented reality glasses, Telepathy One. They're more stylish and have a single piece of metal with a camera and micro-projector.

Telepathy One was unveiled at the South by Southwest festival in Austin, Texas, and has attracted $5m in funding. It's set to launch in 2014, just like Google Glass. However, Iguchi says his device is more focused on communication and sharing. You can connect it to your phone via Bluetooth and share photos and videos from your line of vision on Facebook or send them as an email.

Iguchi wants Telepathy One to bring people closer together. He believes that with this device, you can understand others better by seeing their point of view - literally and metaphorically. Iguchi has worked in the Japanese tech industry for 20 years and developed a location-based phone app called Sekai Camera.

Although Google is a big competitor, Iguchi is not intimidated. He quotes Sun Tzu's The Art of War, saying that even small armies can beat powerful forces. Iguchi moved from Tokyo to Silicon Valley to compete globally. He's putting together a team of software engineers in the US and will make the hardware in Japan.

Google's vice-president Vint Cerf has warned that many digital files may be lost forever because the programs needed to view them will become outdated. This could mean that future historians will not have access to important information from our past, including emails, tweets, and videos. Cerf calls this problem "bit rot," where old computer files become useless.

Cerf is worried that we are losing our digital history because we don't have a way to preserve old software and hardware. He suggests creating "digital vellum" to store these old systems so that we can still access out-of-date files in the future. Cerf believes that if we want to keep our digital lives, we need to make sure that the digital objects we create today can still be used far into the future.

The problem of bit rot is not just about accessing old files; it's also about understanding them. In the past, people wrote on clay tablets or papyrus scrolls that could be read with just eyes. Today, we have many different file types that need special software and hardware to interpret. This makes it difficult for future scholars to study our culture.

Cerf is not just worried about losing old games and videos; he's also concerned about important historical documents. It seems to get easier for a bit, but then my heart starts pounding and I know I won't last much longer. I let out a tiny breath, which helps, but eventually, I have to breathe again. My record is one minute and 12 seconds.

Breath-holding is important in some sports, like freediving. In 2006, I met Sam Amps, the captain of the UK freedive team. She taught me exercises to help me hold my breath longer while swimming underwater. By the end of our session, I could hold my breath for 90 seconds and swim a width. Sam could hold her breath for five minutes and swim three widths easily.

I asked Sam how she did it. She said she breathed slowly before diving, took a deep breath, and trained to resist the urge to breathe. Some people think that humans can hold their breath because we evolved from aquatic animals. However, this idea is not supported by scientific evidence.

It turns out that many non-aquatic mammals can also hold their breath. When we hold our breath on land, our heart rate doesn't slow down. But when we're underwater and our face gets cold, our heart rate does slow down. This is called the "mammalian diving reflex."

Our ability to hold our breath might not be unique, but it's useful in medicine. For example, radiotherapy for breast cancer requires patients to stay still for several minutes. If they can hold their breath, doctors can deliver the entire dose of radiation at once.

Paul Edmondson from the Shakespeare Birthplace Trust argues that Stratford played a significant role in Shakespeare's life. Shakespeare is widely regarded as the most famous playwright in the world, despite what 17th-century writer John Aubrey thought. Despite being famous during his lifetime, there is limited documentary evidence about Shakespeare's life. However, his friends and fellow actors collected his plays and published them in the First Folio in 1623. Many of these surviving copies will be on display, including those from the British and Bodleian libraries. An exhibition at Somerset House in London will feature some of the most precious documents related to Shakespeare's life, including four of his known signatures.

In just ten years, Facebook has changed many things, including how we relate to each other, our privacy, businesses, news media, and even governments.

Mark Zuckerberg believes that a more open and connected world is better for everyone. He thinks it brings stronger relationships, a stronger economy with more opportunities, and a society that reflects all of our values.

Here are some ways Facebook has changed the world:

1. Facebook has changed what we mean by "friend". Now, you can easily add or remove friends online, which is different from real life. You can also see what your friends are doing without having to ask them. However, this has also made it easier for people to end friendships.

Professor Robin Dunbar says that humans can only have about 150 close relationships. Facebook hasn't changed this, but it's made it easier for people to stop being friends with someone online. This might mean we don't learn how to get along with others as well.

2. We care less about our privacy on Facebook. Many users are willing to share their personal information, such as photos and addresses, even though they know that Facebook uses this information to make money. Young people are especially willing to share their details online.

3. Facebook has created many jobs, but not just for its own employees. It's also helped create a whole industry of people who work with brands to use the platform effectively. 4. Facebook has been used to organize revolutions and protests.

The last major United Nations assessment in 2007 predicted a huge temperature rise of 6°C or more by the end of the century. However, scientists now think this is unlikely. This would be enough to devastate crops and make life in many cities unbearably hot.

East Africa can expect more short rains, while west Africa should prepare for heavier monsoons. Countries like Burma, Bangladesh, and India may experience stronger cyclones. In southern Asia, summer rains are expected to be heavier.

The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) report says that global precipitation will change in the long term. High-latitude countries like those in Europe or North America can expect more rainfall. However, many subtropical arid and semi-arid regions will likely receive less rain. In wet tropical regions, extreme rainfall events will be more intense and frequent.

Scientists also predict changes in monsoon patterns. Monsoons may start earlier or not change much, but they will last longer. Scientists in developing countries welcome the report, saying it confirms their own observations of climate change.

Some men go through a difficult time when they feel unhappy and uncertain about their future. This is often called a "midlife crisis." But it's not just humans who might experience this - scientists think that some animals, like chimpanzees and orangutans, may also go through a similar phase.

A team of researchers from around the world studied over 500 apes in zoos and sanctuaries. They asked the people who care for these animals to fill out questionnaires about their behavior and mood. The questions included how much the apes enjoyed socializing and whether they were successful at achieving certain goals.

The results showed that, just like humans, middle-aged apes tend to be less happy than younger or older ones. This dip in happiness happened around age 28-35 for chimpanzees and orangutans. The researchers think this might be because the apes are aware of their own mortality or because of changes in their brains that happen as they get older.

One of the researchers, Alex Weiss, believes that studying animals can help us understand why some humans experience a midlife crisis. "If we want to find out what's going on with the midlife crisis, we should look at what is similar in middle-aged humans, chimps, and orangutans," he said.

However, not all scientists agree with these findings. Some think that the idea of a midlife crisis is exaggerated or doesn't exist at all. Brazil and Peru say a private company shouldn't own a name that refers to an important geographical area that spans their countries. They think it's not in the public interest to let companies register geographical names as top-level domains just to promote their brand or make money.

Not one of these sites was unaffected by human noise, such as planes flying overhead or traffic. A recent poll named McDonald's hamburgers the worst in America, with diners preferring Five Guys or Smashburger. McDonald's is also seen as less healthy than its competitors, especially Chipotle, which emphasizes antibiotic-free meat and locally sourced produce.

To address consumer concerns, McDonald's launched a website to answer questions about its food. But this effort has exposed deep mistrust among consumers. Some asked if McDonald's uses "pink slime" (a beef filler made from gristle and fat) in its burgers or if its beef contains worms. The company has denied these claims.
