Amazon says it's close to using drones to deliver packages. But others are not so sure. They think there are still many technical problems to solve before this can happen safely.

Paul Misener, Amazon's vice-president of global public policy, recently told a congressional hearing that his company is ready to start as soon as the rules are in place. However, he didn't give any details about what those rules would look like.

The Federal Aviation Authority (FAA) will have regulations for using drones commercially by June 2016. But even then, only small drones weighing up to 25kg will be allowed. Larger machines won't be permitted yet.

Professor Sajiv Singh of Carnegie Mellon University Robotics Institute says that flying a drone is not as simple as it sounds. Even short flights can pose serious problems, such as avoiding obstacles and finding the right route. "They're proposing to deliver from a warehouse to an urban or suburban area," he said. "There will be hazards along the way that the vehicle has to detect."

Another problem is maintaining radio contact with the drone. If the connection breaks, the drone could crash. This is not a hard problem to fix, but it's not yet standard practice.

Jay McConville of Lockheed Martin says that you can't do everything with a small 25kg aircraft. His company has been working on making drone piloting interfaces easier to use.

Daniel Huber, a roboticist at Carnegie Mellon University, is working on a program that uses drones to inspect infrastructure. He thinks that most of the technology needed for this is already in place.

Waiters at PizzaExpress are angry and want the public's support. They are protesting because the company takes 8p from every £1 customers tip when they pay by card. The waiters think this is unfair and that the company should give them all of their tips.

PizzaExpress has over 430 restaurants in the UK and makes around £1 million a year from taking a percentage of tips. The company says it uses this money to cover its costs, but the union Unite disagrees. Unite represents many PizzaExpress workers and is organizing the protests.

One waiter said that she loses £3 per night because of the 8% deduction. She has worked at PizzaExpress for 15 years and still only earns the minimum wage of £6.50 an hour. She relies on tips to make a living, but feels that the company is taking money from her.

PizzaExpress is not the only restaurant chain that takes a percentage of tips. Some chains take even more than 8%. However, some restaurants do not take any percentage of tips at all.

A spokesperson for PizzaExpress said that the company's system for distributing tips is fair and that the admin charge covers its costs. But Unite says that this is not true and that the company is making a profit from the admin fee.

The union has started an online petition, which over 5,000 people have signed so far. They are also targeting other restaurant chains that take a percentage of tips. Conservative MP Andrew Percy plans to raise the issue in parliament after the summer recess.

Some restaurants do not deduct any admin fees from tips. These include Wagamama, Pizza Hut, and TGI Friday. The Restaurant Group used to charge 10% but stopped doing so several years

The National Security Agency (NSA) has gained direct access to the systems of major US internet companies, including Google, Facebook, and Apple. This access is part of a secret program called PRISM, which allows officials to collect data such as search history, email content, file transfers, and live chats.

The Guardian verified the authenticity of a top-secret document that describes the program. The document claims that the NSA collects data directly from the servers of major US service providers with their assistance. However, when asked for comment, these companies denied any knowledge of the program.

Google stated that it discloses user data to the government only in accordance with the law and reviews such requests carefully. Other senior tech executives also claimed they had no knowledge of PRISM or similar schemes.

The NSA's access was made possible by changes to US surveillance laws introduced under President Bush and renewed under Obama in 2012. The program allows for extensive surveillance on live communications and stored information, targeting customers outside the US or Americans communicating with people abroad.

The disclosure of PRISM follows a leak about a top-secret court order requiring Verizon to hand over phone records of millions of US customers. Unlike this earlier leak, PRISM involves collecting content from communications, not just metadata.

Major internet companies have been part of PRISM since its introduction in 2007, including Microsoft, Yahoo, Google, Facebook, and Apple. The program allows the NSA direct access to these companies' servers, enabling it to collect data without needing individual court orders or consent from service providers.

A chart prepared by the NSA highlights the range of data it can obtain through PRISM, including emails, videos, photos, and social networking details. A senior administration official stated that the program is subject to oversight and

Do you want your child to be good at sports and maybe even compete internationally? Research suggests that children born in November or October have an advantage. A study by Dr Gavin Sandercock from Essex University found that school pupils born in these months are fitter than their classmates.

The research involved 8,550 boys and girls aged 10-16 from 26 state schools in Essex. They were tested on three measures of fitness: stamina, handgrip strength, and lower-body power. The results showed that children born in autumn (September to November) had a clear physical advantage over those born in other months.

November-born children were the fittest overall, with the most stamina and power, and were the second strongest. Those born in October were almost as fit, scoring highest for strength and coming third for power. The gap between children born in different months was sometimes very wide. For example, a boy born in November can run 10% faster, jump 12% higher, and is 15% more powerful than a child of the same age born in April.

The study found that when scores for the three kinds of fitness were combined, those born in April were the least fit, followed by those in June. This could mean that these children are less likely to be selected for school teams and may not reach their full sporting potential.

The researchers believe that autumn-born children's greater exposure to vitamin D during pregnancy is the most likely explanation for their physical advantage. Vitamin D is linked to a range of health benefits and is often referred to as the "sunshine vitamin".

John Steele, chief executive of the Youth Sport Trust, said that a high-quality introduction to PE and sport at school can also play a major role in a child

Kate Bush is performing live again after 35 years, but this time she's asking her fans not to use their phones during the show. When she last performed, mobile phones were still being tested and didn't exist in public hands. Now, most concerts are filled with people watching through screens.

Before her London shows at the Hammersmith Apollo, Bush asked her fans on her website to put away their phones. She wants an "intimate" experience with her audience, not with iPhones or cameras. Bush chose a smaller theater for this reason and hopes fans will respect her wish.

Bush isn't the only artist who feels this way. Many musicians think that phones at concerts are a problem. Roger Daltrey from The Who said it's "weird" when people stare at screens instead of watching the show. He thinks they're missing out on half of the experience.

Beyoncé once told a fan to stop filming during a concert, saying, "You can't even sing because you're too busy taping." Jarvis Cocker and Johnny Marr have also spoken out against phones at concerts. They think fans are wasting their time by watching through small screens instead of enjoying the live music.

Some artists have tried to ban phones or asked fans not to film during shows. The Yeah Yeah Yeahs put up a sign asking fans to pocket their technology, while pianist Krystian Zimerman stormed off stage because someone was filming him.

The world's top water scientists have issued a severe warning about the global food supply. They say that by 2050, people may need to switch to a mostly vegetarian diet to avoid severe food shortages. Currently, humans get around 20% of their protein from animal products, but this might need to drop to just 5% to feed the extra two billion people expected to be alive by then.

According to research by Malik Falkenmark and colleagues at the Stockholm International Water Institute (SIWI), there won't be enough water available on current farmland to produce food for the expected nine-billion population in 2050 if we continue with our current eating habits. However, if we limit animal-based foods to just 5% of total calories, there will be just enough water.

This warning comes as Oxfam and the UN prepare for a possible second global food crisis in five years. Food prices have risen nearly 50% on international markets since June due to severe droughts in the US and Russia, and weak monsoon rains in Asia. Over 18 million people are already facing serious food shortages across the Sahel region.

Oxfam predicts that this price spike will have a devastating impact on developing countries that rely heavily on food imports. Food shortages in 2008 led to civil unrest in 28 countries. Adopting a vegetarian diet is one way to increase the amount of water available for growing more food, as animal protein-rich foods consume five to ten times more water than a vegetarian diet.

The city of Kiruna in northern Sweden is facing a unique problem - it needs to move to avoid being destroyed by an iron-ore mine that is causing the ground beneath its streets to collapse. The city, home to 23,000 people, was founded in 1900 and has grown rich from the vast seam of iron ore below it. However, the mine's expansion now threatens the city's very existence.

Kiruna is located inside the Arctic Circle and has a harsh climate with long winters and extremely cold temperatures. Despite this, the city has thrived due to the mine, which produces 90% of Europe's iron ore. The demand for iron continues to grow, but the mining company warned the town in 2004 that its days were numbered.

The city has been living in uncertainty for ten years, with residents unable to make major decisions about their lives. A master plan has finally been unveiled, which involves moving the entire city eastwards along a new high street by 2033. The plan includes building a new town square, dismantling and reassembling key buildings, and creating a new park.

However, not everything will be saved, and many residents are concerned about losing their sense of identity and community. The project has been allocated £320m for building new facilities, but the details of housing allocation have yet to be determined. Residents are worried that they won't be able to afford new homes, despite being compensated by the mining company.

The architects behind the plan believe it's an opportunity for Kiruna to reinvent itself as a model of sustainable development, attracting young people and creating new cultural facilities. However, many existing residents seem unlikely to be able to afford this vision. The city is facing a difficult decision

US researchers have shown how government surveillance programs that collect phone records can threaten people's personal privacy. Two scientists at Stanford University used basic phone logs to identify individuals and uncover confidential information about their lives.

The researchers had access to anonymous "metadata" on people's calls and texts, but not the content of the communications. They were able to work out individuals' names, where they lived, and the names of their partners. They also uncovered sensitive information about some individuals, such as one man who owned a rifle and another who had an irregular heartbeat.

The study highlights the power of telephone metadata, which includes the number called, when, and for how long. This data can be paired with public information from services like Google, Yelp, and Facebook to reveal a lot about someone's life. The security services have long recognized the value of this data, but it is not subject to the same legal protections as the content of people's communications.

The researchers collected metadata from 823 people who agreed to participate in the study. They gathered information on over 250,000 calls and 1.2 million texts. By analyzing this data, they were able to identify 82% of people's names and the names of businesses they had called. They also used this information to locate where people lived, with a high degree of accuracy.

The researchers then looked at more personal information, such as who was in a relationship. They used a computer program to analyze call patterns and inferred who among the study volunteers was in a relationship. Once they knew someone had a partner, identifying the significant other was easy.

Angela Erdmann never met her grandfather because he died in 1946, six years before she was born. But on April 8th, 2014, something amazing happened. She received a message in a bottle that her grandfather had thrown into the Baltic Sea 101 years earlier. This is believed to be the world's oldest message in a bottle.

The museum in Germany where the bottle is now on display gave it to Erdmann. "It was very surprising," she said, remembering how she found out about the bottle. A man came to her door and told her he had a letter from her grandfather. He explained that a fisherman had found a message in a bottle with her grandfather's name on it.

The brown beer bottle had been in the water for 101 years. It was found by Konrad Fischer, a fisherman who was out in the Baltic Sea near the city of Kiel. The museum curator, Holger von Neuhoff, said this is the oldest message in a bottle he has ever seen. "There are older documents without bottles that we have in the museum," he said. "But with the bottle and the document together, this is certainly the oldest."

Researchers think Erdmann's grandfather, Richard Platz, threw the bottle into the sea during a hike in 1913. He was 20 years old at the time. The postcard inside the bottle was mostly unreadable, but the address on the front was clear. So was the message asking whoever found it to send it back to him.

You're standing in line at a store when you notice the person next to you is acting strangely. They're not holding a shopping list, but instead have handwritten notes about the store's appearance and cleanliness. They're also timing how long it takes for the line to move on their phone, and there might even be a small camera hidden in their purse. It's likely that this person is a mystery shopper.

In the UK, around 50,000 mystery shopping trips are carried out every month. As more people shop online, stores want to know how they can improve the experience for customers who visit in person. Simon Boydell from Marketforce says, "Retailers want to measure how well their stores deliver on that experience." Marketforce has over 300,000 mystery shoppers and assigns them different store locations to visit.

Mystery shoppers typically spend up to eight hours a day visiting five to ten stores, and then another hour or two writing detailed reports about each visit. They can earn up to £155 per day, plus reimbursement for petrol and hotel stays. Some mystery shoppers even use hidden cameras to film their visits and can earn around £300 per day.

Mystery shoppers are usually given money to spend in the stores they visit, and they might get to keep the products they buy. Laura, a 50-year-old mystery shopper from Devon, has visited over 7,000 shops since 2001. She's paid to assess the service she receives at the till and is often given £5-£20 to spend in each store.

Over a million workers in Britain might be employed on zero-hours contracts, according to new figures. This suggests that British businesses are using these contracts more widely than previously thought. 

The Chartered Institute of Personnel and Development (CIPD) conducted a poll of over 1,000 employers to get this figure. The result has led to renewed calls for the government to investigate the use of zero-hours contracts. Many organizations have faced criticism recently for hiring staff without guaranteeing work or pay each week.

Workers on zero-hours contracts often don't receive holiday or sick pay and need permission to look for additional work elsewhere. Despite this, 38% of workers on these contracts consider themselves full-time employees, typically working over 30 hours a week. One-third of voluntary sector employers use zero-hours contracts, as do one in four public sector organizations.

The new figures also question the accuracy of official data on zero-hours contracts. The Office for National Statistics has increased its estimate of UK zero-hours workers by 25%, to around 250,000.

Peter Cheese, CEO of the CIPD, said: "We need a closer look at what zero-hours contracts mean and how they are used in practice." He added that there needs to be clearer guidance on good and bad practices for both businesses and employees.

Several companies have recently faced criticism for using zero-hours contracts. Sports Direct employs around 20,000 staff on these contracts, while pub group J D Wetherspoon has 24,000 staff – 80% of its workforce – on similar terms.

Vidhya Alakeson from the Resolution Foundation said: "If one million people are on zero-hours contracts, that's a significant portion of the workforce. The government needs to review

Tigers are now more numerous in Nepal than they have been since the 1970s, according to a new census. This gives conservationists hope that these big cats can be saved. The number of wild royal Bengal tigers in Nepal has increased by 63.6% over five years and is now at 198.

The government survey used pictures from more than 500 cameras placed in protected areas and wildlife corridors. Over 250 experts worked on the survey, which cost around £250,000. An ecologist with Nepal's Department of National Parks and Wildlife Conservation said, "This is very encouraging."

A similar survey was conducted in India, and the results will be published later this year. Nepal has promised to double its tiger population by 2022 from 121 in 2009. However, increasing prosperity in Asia has led to higher prices for tiger skins and body parts used in traditional Chinese medicines.

International gangs pay local Nepalis significant amounts of money to kill tigers. The skin and bones are then passed on to middlemen who take them across the border into India. One major problem is that some senior officials are involved with these mafia networks.

Conservation experts believe that effective policing, stronger anti-poaching efforts, and better management of tiger habitats have contributed to the increase in numbers. However, they say Nepal needs to do more to protect the habitat and animals that tigers prey on.

As the number of tigers has increased, so have incidents of conflict with villagers. In 2012, seven people were killed by tigers around national parks, compared to four in 2011. Villagers are seeking better protection from the government.

Wildlife authorities recently captured a tiger after it killed two people in Chitwan

Louise Haggerty, a 56-year-old hairdresser and waitress, went to Sainsbury's supermarket in Harringay, north-east London for the Black Friday sales. She arrived at 1 am with a friend, hoping to buy a flat-screen TV on sale. However, she was shocked by the chaos inside the store. "It was mental in there," she said. "People were behaving like animals – it was horrible."

Haggerty and her friend tried to queue for the TV, but many people pushed in front of them. A woman who was second in line was even pushed out by a group of young men. Haggerty only saw two security guards trying to control the crowd.

Frustrated, Haggerty grabbed a Dyson vacuum cleaner that was on sale instead. "I don't even know how much it costs; I don't know if I'm going to buy it," she said. "There are people in there with three or four TVs. It's not fair."

Andy Blackett, an estate agent, had more success. He and his friends arrived at 12:45 am and managed to grab several bargains, including two coffee makers, two tablets, two TVs, and a stereo.

However, the situation was different at Tesco's 24-hour Lea Valley supermarket, where the Black Friday sale started at midnight. The store became chaotic, with scuffles breaking out between shoppers. Police officers were called to the scene, and one officer criticized the manager for not having enough security.

The police also intervened at other stores, including Tesco in Willesden and Surrey Quays. Greater Manchester Police reported that two people had been arrested at Black Friday sales events.

Barack Obama has told young people that they can make a difference in the world if they reject pessimism and talk to those who have different beliefs. 
On his last visit to Britain as US president, Obama spoke to 500 youth leaders at a meeting in London. He said: “Don’t think there are things we can’t control. As JFK said, our problems were made by people and can be solved by people.” 
He told the students that they have the best tools ever to make a difference. “Don’t be pessimistic or cynical. Progress is possible but it takes hard work and discipline.” 
Obama knows that young people face many challenges, including big changes in the world since 9/11 and 7/7, and constant bad news on social media. 
The audience cheered as Obama spoke about his policies, such as healthcare and education. He encouraged them to talk to people with different views: “Find people who disagree with you and try to understand their perspective.” 
Obama also said that young people should feel hopeful because social attitudes are changing. However, he added that change is slow and they must keep pushing for it. 
When asked about his time as president, Obama was proud of his healthcare reforms and the US response to the 2008 financial crisis. He also mentioned diplomatic deals with Iran and the response to the Ebola crisis as highlights. “I’m proud of what I’ve done,” he said. 
However, he warned against giving up if progress is slow: “Don’t listen to cynics who say nothing has changed after five years.”

Millennials are known for relying heavily on technology. More than 80% of them sleep with their mobile phone next to their bed, and almost two-thirds admit to texting while driving. Many have also posted videos of themselves online or created social media profiles.

Compared to other generations, millennials use social media the most. A 2010 report found that 75% of millennials had created at least one social media account. In contrast, only 50% of Generation X and 30% of baby boomers use social media.

However, there are some millennials who don't use social media at all. Celan Beausoleil, a 31-year-old social worker from California, is one example. She had an "on and off" relationship with Facebook but eventually deactivated her account in 2015. She found it overwhelming to see so much personal information shared by others on top of her work demands.

Beausoleil does appreciate the way social media connects people around the world. However, she realized that she was spending too much time scrolling through Facebook and decided to focus on other things instead.

Another millennial who quit social media is Mathias from Baltimore. He deleted his Facebook and Twitter accounts in 2012 and hasn't looked back. While he acknowledges the benefits of social media, such as organizing events online, he prefers to spend his free time reading news articles and books.

Lauren Raskauskas, a 22-year-old from Florida, is also not a fan of social media. She describes herself as a "private person" and doesn't like sharing her personal life with others online. She recently deleted her Twitter account and deactivated her Facebook account due to concerns about data privacy.

Large predators like brown bears, wolves, and lynx are thriving in Europe's forests and suburbs, despite concerns about human population growth and overconsumption. A new study published in Science found that these animals' populations are stable or increasing on the crowded continent.

Brown bears, wolves, Eurasian lynx, and wolverines can be found in nearly one-third of mainland Europe (excluding Belarus, Ukraine, and Russia). Most of these animals live outside nature reserves, showing that changing attitudes and conservation efforts are working. Bears are the most common large carnivore in Europe, with around 17,000 individuals, followed by 12,000 wolves, 9,000 Eurasian lynx, and 1,250 wolverines.

Only a few countries in mainland Europe, such as Belgium and Denmark, have no breeding populations of these animals. However, researchers believe that even densely populated areas can support large predators. In some cases, wolves live in suburban areas with up to 3,050 people per square kilometer.

The study's lead author, Guillaume Chapron, says that this shows a "land-sharing" model of conservation is working. This approach involves managing conflicts between humans and animals rather than separating them. Chapron notes that coexistence can be challenging, but it's possible to resolve problems and keep conflict levels low.

The success of this approach in Europe is attributed to factors like political stability, growing prey populations, and financial support for non-lethal livestock protection. The EU Habitats Directive has also played a crucial role in protecting and reviving rare species.

The view from the visitors' centre at Doñana National Park in southern Spain is breathtaking. This park is a haven for birds, with 200,000 hectares of salt marsh that are crucial for western Europe's birdlife. Many migratory birds from Britain, such as house martins and swallows, rest here on their way to Africa. The park is also home to some of Europe's rarest birds, including the Spanish imperial eagle, and endangered animals like the Iberian lynx.

However, this beautiful landscape is fragile. In 1998, a dam burst at Los Frailes mine, releasing two billion gallons of toxic water into the park. This caused Spain's worst environmental disaster, killing over 25,000 fish and nearly 2,000 birds. The clean-up cost €90m.

After this disaster, Spain invested €360m in restoring the landscape, which had been damaged by farming and drainage. Some farmland is being returned to its natural wetland state. This process has been costly but successful.

Despite this progress, Doñana still faces many threats. Plans have been proposed to build an oil pipeline through the park, and tourist resorts may expand, putting pressure on the local water supply. Silt from nearby farms is also harming the park's channels.

The biggest concern for conservationists is the decision to reopen Los Frailes mine, which caused the 1998 disaster. "This is Europe's most important bird sanctuary," says Laurence Rose of the RSPB. "Reopening the mine would be extremely worrying."

In the UK, there is no law that says restaurants must give tips to their staff. This was discovered in a government review in 2016, where workers, employers, and customers shared their thoughts on tipping. The government wants to change this and make sure low-paid workers get the money left for them by customers.

Some waiters are charged up to 15% of their tips as an administration fee when customers pay by card. In some cases, waiters have to give their own money if they don't collect enough tips to cover these fees. The government wants to stop employers from charging workers these fees.

The government also wants restaurants to be more open about their tipping policies. They want customers to know that tips are voluntary and for restaurants to clearly display how tips are shared among staff.

We spoke to waiters around the UK to find out what they think of the tipping system. Here's what they said:

Rodri, 37, from London, says that around 50% of a waiter's income comes from tips. He thinks the US has a fairer system, where customers are more likely to tip. Rodri can earn up to £100 in tips per shift, but sometimes it's as low as £40.

Elle, 22, from Edinburgh, says that waiters never know if they're getting a fair share of tips. She works three jobs and thinks the system is better in France, where waiting tables is seen as a proper job with good pay and security.

Ashley, 22, from London, says that tips are often used to cover breakages caused by customers. He thinks it's unfair that staff have to pay for mistakes made by others. Ashley earns around £10-15 per shift

A traditional British meal might include a cup of tea, baked beans on toast, or fish and chips. However, people's tastes have changed over time. A recent study by the National Food Survey shows how eating habits have shifted since 1940.

The survey found that tea consumption has decreased significantly. In the 1970s, people drank an average of 68g of tea per week, but this number has dropped to 25g today. This means Britons now drink around eight cups of tea a week, down from 23 cups in 1974. Although tea is still the most popular hot drink, households spend more money on coffee.

The study also shows that people are making healthier choices. There's been an increase in low-calorie soft drinks and skimmed milk consumption. Fresh fruit intake has risen by 50% since 1974, with adults now eating around 157g of fruit per day. Bananas have become the most popular fruit, followed by apples and oranges.

However, there are also some negative trends. Consumption of chips, pizza, crisps, and ready meals has increased significantly. Adults in the UK now eat an average of 75g of pizza every week, compared to none in 1974. Pasta consumption has almost tripled over the same period.

The survey found that people's eating habits are changing due to various factors. There's been a shift from white bread to brown and wholemeal bread, but overall bread consumption has decreased. Baked beans in sauce have become less popular, while Italian dishes like pasta and pizza have gained popularity.

Takeaway food consumption has almost doubled since 1974, with chips being the most popular takeaway item. Other popular takeaway foods include kebabs

Agios Efstratios is a remote Greek island that has been largely forgotten by banks and the government. The mobile phone network doesn't work well here, and there are no ATMs or credit-card machines on the island. Before Greece's financial crisis, residents managed fine without these modern conveniences. They did their banking at the post office, and tourists came to enjoy the island's beautiful beaches, clear seas, and fresh seafood.

However, since the island relies heavily on cash, the closure of banks nationwide has been devastating. Residents have to travel nine hours round-trip to get cash from a nearby island. Greek visitors say they can't afford to come because they don't have enough money. As a result, tourist numbers are down 80% this year.

The mayor, Maria Kakali, has asked the government and a major bank to install an ATM on the island, but it may be too late for this season. The island's economy relies heavily on tourism, fishing, and agriculture. With almost no reservations in August, usually the peak tourist month, the future looks bleak.

To make matters worse, the government plans to end a decades-old tax break for islands like Agios Efstratios. This tax break was created to help island communities survive when many people left to find work elsewhere. If the tax break ends, the island will have to pay 23% sales tax, which would be catastrophic.

Food and fuel are already expensive on the island because everything has to be imported. There are only three shops, two restaurants, and no official hotels. The mayor fears that if the tax break ends, the island's economy will collapse.

Scientists have made a major breakthrough by connecting the brains of two animals, allowing them to share information and work together on simple tasks. This achievement is a step towards creating what they call the world's first "organic computer". 

The US team, led by Miguel Nicolelis, fitted two rats with special devices that let them collaborate on tasks to earn rewards, such as water. In one experiment, they linked the brains of two rats separated by thousands of miles - one in North Carolina and the other in Brazil - using the internet.

Nicolelis said their work may enable multiple brains to be connected to share information. "We have established a direct communication linkage between brains," he said. "We are creating what I call an organic computer."

The scientists first showed that rats can share sensory information by connecting their brains with tiny electrodes. They trained the rats to press a lever when a light came on above it, and rewarded them with water if they did it correctly.

To test the animals' ability to share brain information, they put the rats in separate compartments. Only one compartment had a light that came on above the lever. When the rat pressed the lever, its brain activity was sent directly to the other rat's brain. The second rat responded correctly 70% of the time by pressing the lever.

The communication between the rats was two-way. If the receiving rat failed at the task, the first rat changed its behavior to make it easier for its partner. In further experiments, the rats worked together on a task that required them to distinguish between narrow and wide openings using their whiskers.

Thousands of Australians protested on beaches against killing sharks in Western Australia. They asked the state's leader to stop the killings, which started after several shark attacks along the coast. In 2013, a surfer was killed by a shark, making him the sixth person to die from a shark attack in two years.

However, on average, only one person dies from a shark attack each year in Australia. Kate Faehrmann from the Sea Shepherd Conservation Society said that killing sharks won't work and will also harm other animals like dolphins and turtles. She added that Australians want to protect sharks.

Protests took place on beaches in several cities, including Perth, Sydney, and Adelaide. Faehrmann said that the protests show that many Australians care about sharks and don't want them killed. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has asked the US government to sort out its finances after a 16-day government shutdown ended. The US had come close to defaulting on its debt, but a last-minute deal prevented this.

US President Barack Obama warned that the country must stop governing by crisis. IMF Managing Director Christine Lagarde agreed, saying it's essential to reduce uncertainty around fiscal policy. She also encouraged the US to approve a budget for 2014 and adopt a balanced long-term plan.

The shutdown ended when the Senate and House of Representatives passed a bill to fund the government until January 15 and raise the debt ceiling until February 7. The deal was reached just hours before the deadline to extend the US debt limit.

The World Bank's president, Jim Yong Kim, expressed relief that the global economy had avoided a potential disaster. He urged policymakers to focus on promoting economic growth and creating jobs.

Stock markets in Asia initially reacted positively to the news, but later showed a muted reaction as traders expected another battle in Washington early next year. The shutdown is estimated to have cost the US $24 billion.

China's official news agency had accused the US of putting other countries' dollar assets at risk. China is the US government's largest creditor. Obama signed the bill to prevent default shortly after midnight on Thursday.

The president hopes that the deal will "lift the cloud of uncertainty" that has hung over the country in recent weeks. He also made it clear that he does not expect another bitter budget fight and shutdown in 2014.

Sudan is 42 years old and breeding efforts have failed so far. There are only two other northern white rhinos left, both females in zoos.

Sudan is guarded by armed men who protect him from poachers. These poachers kill rhinos for their horns, which they sell on the Asian medicine market. Even though Sudan's horn has been cut off, he is still at risk. His eyes are sad and his massive face is wrinkled as he walks around the reserve with his guards.

Sudan's head is strong and powerful, but also vulnerable. He looks like an old warrior who is tired of fighting. His legs are short and stick out from his big body. People have been amazed by rhinos for centuries. In 1515, a Renaissance artist named Albrecht Dürer drew a picture of a rhinoceros that looked similar to Sudan.

Humans have a history of killing the things we love. We have been doing this since the Ice Age. There are pictures of woolly rhinos in caves in France that were painted up to 30,000 years ago. These ancient relatives of Sudan were also big and powerful, but gentle. However, humans helped kill them off with spears.

James Bond is one of the most successful film franchises in history, with 23 movies and over $6 billion earned worldwide. Despite its long run, the series shows no signs of slowing down. In fact, after the huge success of Skyfall, which became the biggest film at the UK box office in 2012 and earned $1.1 billion globally, the Bond brand is stronger than ever.

The latest Bond film, Spectre, has generated a lot of interest, with many wondering if it can repeat the success of Skyfall. Charles Gant, film editor for Heat magazine, thinks it's heading in the right direction. "Skyfall was a clever move," he says. "It appealed to both old and new fans." With the same writers and director as Skyfall, Eon Productions is trying to ensure that lightning strikes twice.

Daniel Craig has signed on for at least one more Bond film, and Sam Mendes, who directed Skyfall, is back behind the camera. The success of Skyfall was a significant improvement over its predecessor, Quantum of Solace, which earned $586 million worldwide.

The Bond series has had its ups and downs over the years. After Pierce Brosnan's run, the series felt stale, but the arrival of Daniel Craig and Sam Mendes brought new energy to the franchise. The history of Bond is one of renewal and change, with each new lead actor bringing a fresh perspective.

Factory owners are demanding compensation for the costs of closing and repairing their buildings. Some repair programs will take months to complete, and factory owners say they cannot afford to pay staff while their factories are closed. They also need to pay for major repairs to make sure their buildings are safe.

The agreement, known as the Accord on Fire and Building Safety in Bangladesh, was created after a devastating accident in 2013. The Rana Plaza complex in Dhaka collapsed, killing 1,138 people. The Accord inspects hundreds of Bangladeshi clothing factories every month for fire safety and structural problems. However, some factory owners are unhappy with the agreement. His factory was closed due to structural problems, and he is demanding $100m in compensation.

Another factory owner said that if a factory closes, even temporarily, it will lose orders and eventually shut down permanently. He claimed that the Accord did not clearly address who would pay for factory closures. Jenny Holdcroft, policy director for IndustriALL, disagreed. She said that brands had committed to maintaining orders with suppliers for two years, ensuring that factories would not lose business during closure.

The world's richest 100 billionaires have made huge fortunes that are increasing inequality and making it harder to reduce poverty, according to Oxfam. 
The charity says the massive accumulation of wealth and income by these individuals often comes at the expense of secure jobs and decent wages for the poorest people. This makes it difficult for those living on aid or low wages to improve their situation and escape poverty. 

If the richest 100 billionaires gave away the money they made in 2012, Oxfam says it would be enough to lift the world's poorest people out of poverty several times over. The charity is not pointing fingers at specific individuals but notes that the $240 billion net income earned by these billionaires in 2012 could make extreme poverty history four times over.

While some US billionaires like Bill Gates and Warren Buffett have pledged to give away much of their wealth, others from Russia, the Middle East, and China have not followed suit. Oxfam is calling on world leaders to reduce income extremes and commit to reducing inequality to at least 1990 levels in its report "The Cost of Inequality: How Wealth and Income Extremes Hurt Us All".

The report found that the richest 1% have increased their incomes by 60% over the past 20 years, with the financial crisis making things worse. Oxfam's Chief Executive Barbara Stocking says extreme wealth is not only unfair but also bad for the economy, politics, and society as a whole.

She notes that countries where workers earn less tend to have lower investment and growth rates. "We can no longer pretend that creating wealth for a few will benefit everyone – often it's the opposite," she said.

The issue of inequality affects all parts of the world.

The prime minister promised big changes across Great Britain, including giving English MPs more power over English issues. He welcomed Scotland's decision to remain in the UK and said, "We have heard the clear will of the Scottish people."

Pope Benedict XVI stepped down as the leader of the Catholic Church on a cold February day in 2013. He had been pope since 2005 and was the first German pope in modern times. In his own words, he arrived as "a simple, humble worker in God's vineyard." When he left, it was like an elderly laborer who could no longer do his job due to old age.

Sanchéz Barba described the scene: "We were all in shock... The cardinals just looked at each other." Sanchéz Barba said it was a simple but sad moment.

The Vatican praised the Pope's decision as brave, saying he was facing reality and acknowledging that he was no longer up to running the church.

The Pope himself explained that he needed both physical and mental strength to lead the church, but in recent months, his health had declined. Other theories about his resignation will likely emerge, but the Vatican is expected to dismiss them.

Zimarco Jones, a Nigerian refugee who arrived in Calais in 2013, founded the school with the help of volunteers from Calais and beyond. The school now offers classes in French, English, art, and t'ai chi.

Karim said, "I haven't fainted once," but acknowledged that the long days can be tough. Many Muslims in Iqaluit follow the Ramadan schedule of Ottawa, which is about 1,300 miles south. This means fasting for around 18 hours a day, according to Atif Jilani, who moved from Toronto in 2015.

The community often gathers at the new mosque for nightly suppers, where they share traditional foods like dates and curries while the sun shines through the windows. The Senate Intelligence Committee has approved a bill that will allow the National Security Agency (NSA) to continue collecting phone records of millions of Americans. The bill, sponsored by Chairwoman Dianne Feinstein, requires the NSA to be more transparent about its collection activities but does not end the practice.

Under the bill, the NSA can collect phone metadata for 90-day periods and keep it on file. Analysts can search through the data if they suspect someone is linked to international terrorism. The bill also allows the NSA to continue surveillance of foreigners who enter the US for up to 72 hours.

Some lawmakers have proposed alternative plans, such as letting phone companies hold the metadata instead of the government. Senator Patrick Leahy has introduced a separate bill that would end domestic phone-records collection altogether.

The Intelligence Committee approved the bill by an 11-4 vote, despite opposition from some members who think it does not go far enough to protect Americans' privacy. Mark Udall said the bill "does not respect our constitutional values" and needs fundamental reform. Ron Wyden added that the bill maintains "business as usual" and is "far from meaningful reform".

Feinstein defended the NSA's bulk collection program, saying it contributes to national security but acknowledged a need to rebuild public trust. The bill includes some improvements to transparency and oversight, such as requiring an annual report on the number of queries made by the NSA.

Independent experts have expressed concern that the bill sets up a showdown with the USA Freedom Act, which would prohibit bulk collection of Americans' phone records. Elizabeth Goitein said the two bills present opposing visions of the relationship between law-abiding Americans and the national security state.

Noise from passing ships may be disturbing animals like killer whales and dolphins more than previously thought. New research shows that this noise could affect their ability to communicate and find food. The low rumble of ships has long been known to disturb large whales, but US researchers have found that there is also persistent noise at higher frequencies. This includes the 20,000Hz frequency where killer whales hear best.

This noise could be making it harder for killer whales to use sound to locate objects like prey and identify their location. Dolphins and porpoises may also be affected in the same way. The findings suggest that this noise could affect the endangered population of killer whales near shipping lanes. There are only 84 killer whales that hunt along the US west coast and into Puget Sound.

Scott Veirs, who led the research, said: "Even a small increase in sound can make it harder for whales to use echolocation. This is worrying because their prey, chinook salmon, is already scarce." The researchers used underwater microphones to measure the noise from about 1,600 ships passing through Haro Strait in Washington State.

The study found that some ships are quieter than others, but on average, the noise level next to all the ships was equivalent to a loud rock concert. However, whales are not usually close to ships and would be subjected to noise levels similar to a lawnmower or vacuum cleaner.

Veirs said scientists have already identified the impact of underwater noise on large whales, but this new research highlights the threat to smaller whales, dolphins, and porpoises. "Ships were thought to produce low-frequency noise, but our study shows that they also raise background noise in high frequencies," he said.

Since the lottery started in 1994, these winners have won a total of £8.5 billion, or an average of £2.8 million each. This has created another 3,780 millionaires among their families and friends. Scientists have analyzed DNA from a 7,000-year-old wisdom tooth found in Spain. This has given them a unique look at what modern humans were like before farming began. The man who owned the tooth was a hunter-gatherer with an unusual combination of blue eyes, dark hair, and dark skin.

He probably had trouble digesting milk and starchy foods, unlike farmers who came later. When people started farming, they came into close contact with animals, which led to the spread of diseases. As a result, humans developed stronger immune systems to fight off these infections. However, scientists may have overestimated how much farming changed the human immune system.

Tests on the hunter-gatherer's DNA showed that he already had genetic mutations that helped his body fight off certain diseases. Some of these mutations are still found in modern Europeans today. The study's leader, Carles Lalueza-Fox, said that many of their initial ideas about what they would find were wrong.

The tooth was discovered in a cave in northwest Spain in 2006. It belonged to one of two skeletons found by cavers. The remains were well-preserved due to the cool environment of the cave. Carbon dating showed that the skeletons were around 7,000 years old, before farming spread from the Middle East to Europe.

The scientists focused on the better-preserved skeleton and managed to reconstruct the man's entire genome from DNA found in his tooth. This is the first time researchers have obtained a complete genome of a modern European who lived before the Neolithic revolution.

Chemists have been waiting a long time for new elements to be discovered. Now, four new ones have been found at the same time. Researchers from Japan, Russia, and the US made this discovery. These new elements are the first to be added to the periodic table since 2011. They complete the seventh row of the table and make science textbooks outdated.

The International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC) verified these elements on December 30, 2015. IUPAC is a global organization that governs chemical names, terms, and measurements. The scientists who discovered these elements must now give them formal names to replace their temporary Latin-based names: ununtrium, ununpentium, ununseptium, and ununoctium.

IUPAC announced that a team of Russian and American scientists had enough evidence to claim the discovery of elements 115, 117, and 118. A Japanese team from the RIKEN Institute discovered element 113. This makes Japan the first Asian country to name an element. According to IUPAC rules, new elements can be named after mythological concepts, minerals, places, countries, or scientists.

When elements 114 and 116 were given formal names in 2012, they were named flerovium and livermorium. The Japanese team is now considering three names for ununtrium: japonium, rikenium, and nishinarium. The scientists must also propose two-letter symbols for the elements.

A new scientific study warns that temperature rises due to climate change will be more severe than expected. The research leader, Professor Steven Sherwood, says that unless greenhouse gas emissions are reduced, the planet will warm by at least 4C by 2100. This is twice the level considered dangerous by world governments.

The study found that as the planet warms, fewer clouds form, allowing less sunlight to be reflected back into space and driving temperatures up further. The role of clouds in global warming has been a major mystery until now. Sherwood says this study makes two important breakthroughs: it identifies what controls cloud changes and rules out lower estimates of future global warming.

A 4C rise would have catastrophic consequences, making life difficult or impossible in many tropical regions. It would also lead to the melting of ice sheets in Greenland and Antarctica, causing sea levels to rise by several meters. The research is a significant advance that reduces uncertainty about how much warming is caused by carbon emissions.

Scientists measure climate sensitivity by estimating the temperature rise caused by a doubling of CO2 in the atmosphere. For 20 years, estimates have ranged from 1.5C to 5C. This study narrows that range to between 3C and 5C by examining clouds, the main cause of uncertainty.

To accurately predict future temperatures, researchers used computer climate models that simulate how clouds form in the real world. They found that models that include complex cloud formation processes predict significantly higher future temperatures than those that do not.

The world is changing fast, and transportation is no exception. Experts agree that economic, demographic, and technological changes are transforming the way people move around cities. Robert Puentes of the Brookings Institution says, "It's a very dynamic time. There's a focus on connecting transportation to the economic health of cities and its impact on people."

As commutes get longer and infrastructure ages, US cities like Los Angeles, Seattle, and Chicago are redefining transportation. They're adding bus lanes, pedestrian walkways, and rail options, while working with private companies on advanced technologies like self-driving cars that can communicate with other vehicles and the environment.

Three key trends will shape the transportation industry in the coming years:

1. Ride-sharing services like Uber and Lyft are changing how people get around, affecting traffic patterns and communication between riders, drivers, and infrastructure.
2. Vehicle travel is declining among millennials, who prefer alternative modes of transport. According to a UCLA study, those born in the 1990s make 4% fewer car trips and travel 18% fewer miles per year than previous generations.
3. Driverless cars are being developed, with partial automation already underway. Experts predict that automation will progress in stages, starting with automated buses and lorries.

The idea of a fully automated transportation system is exciting, as it could improve safety, efficiency, and reduce emissions. However, even if the technology were ready now, it would take time to implement given the average age of cars on the road.

As countries work to meet ambitious emissions goals, policies will likely impact the future of transportation, promoting zero- and low-emission vehicles, walking, biking, and carpooling apps.

Air India will teach yoga to its trainee pilots.

The era of large British summer music festivals like Glastonbury is coming to an end, according to Harvey Goldsmith, a leading rock promoter and manager. 
Goldsmith has worked with many famous musicians, including The Who, The Rolling Stones, Queen, Madonna, Bob Dylan, and Luciano Pavarotti. He believes the main problem is that there are not enough new bands to replace the old ones. 
"The festival circuit has reached its peak," he said at the Hay Festival of Literature and Arts in Wales. "There are too many festivals and not enough big acts to headline them. This is a major issue for our industry." 
In 2014, there were around 900 music festivals in the UK between May and September. Goldsmith thinks that this number cannot be sustained. "Music festivals have probably had their time," he said. "Instead, we will see more events that combine music with other things like poetry, books, or magic shows." 
Goldsmith also believes that the way people listen to music has changed. "People don't want to listen to a whole album anymore," he said. "Most rock bands built their reputation on albums, but young people are not interested in this. They prefer individual tracks and move quickly from one song to another." 
Goldsmith is now working with Dutch producer Robin de Levita on a new 1,100-seat theatre in Wembley. The theatre will feature a unique concept called SceneAround, where the audience seating rotates around a series of scenes accompanied by projections on screens. 
The first production at the theatre will be an adaptation of The Hunger Games book and movie series. Goldsmith is also planning to bring a production of the Anne Frank story to the venue.

The man, dressed only in underpants, told his rescuers that he had set out from Mexico for El Salvador in September 2012. He said a companion had died at sea several months earlier. The man's name was José Ivan, and he claimed to have survived by catching turtles and birds with his bare hands.

The boat had no fishing equipment, but a turtle was found inside when it washed up on the shore. "The boat is really scratched up and looks like it has been in the water for a long time," said Ola Fjeldstad, a Norwegian researcher who met the man.

José Ivan was taken to the main island in the atoll to meet the mayor, Ione de Brum, who contacted the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Officials are waiting for more details and expect José Ivan to be taken to the capital soon. However, the government airline's only plane that can land on the atoll is currently being repaired.

In the meantime, José Ivan is staying with a local family and receiving basic medical care. He had low blood pressure but no life-threatening conditions. "We've been giving him a lot of water, and he's gaining strength," said Fjeldstad.

SeaWorld's profits have fallen by 84% as fewer people visit the theme park due to concerns about its treatment of orca whales. The company trains dolphins and killer whales to perform tricks, but has faced criticism since a documentary called Blackfish was released in 2013. The film claimed that SeaWorld's treatment of orcas led to violent behavior and the deaths of three people.

As a result, attendance at the park has decreased, along with sales and profits. Despite launching a marketing campaign to improve its image, SeaWorld is still struggling to convince the public that it treats its whales well. The company has cut ticket prices and spent $10m on advertising, but CEO Joel Manby admits that more work needs to be done.

Manby said that while some people have responded positively to the campaign, it will take time and investment to fully recover from the damage to the company's reputation. He also stated that SeaWorld will continue to argue its case using facts, as he believes they are on the company's side.

SeaWorld has plans for new attractions, including a shark exhibition in Orlando and an attraction in San Antonio where visitors can swim with dolphins. However, the company's financial report showed a significant decline in net income, from $37.4m to $5.8m, and revenue fell from $405m to $392m.

It was a lovely summer evening when I decided to go for a swim off Doolin Pier in County Clare, Ireland. A woman was already in the water with Dusty, a dolphin who has been visiting the area since 2008 and has become friendly with many people. Hundreds of people have swum with her over the years, making it seem like she's completely tame.

As I got into the water, Dusty suddenly became aggressive and swam towards me. Her tail was flapping wildly, and at first, I thought it was just a show. But then I realized she might be angry. I tried to swim back to the pier, but Dusty hit me with her snout before I could get out of the water. It was very painful and happened so fast.

The people on the pier were shocked and staring at me in amazement. Dusty was still beside me, flapping her tail wildly, which made me even more scared. I thought that if she hit me again with her tail, I could drown. I shouted for help, and a man pulled me out of the water.

Luckily, an orthopedic surgeon happened to be driving by and saw what had happened. He checked my injuries and reassured me that he didn't think I was bleeding internally, but I probably had broken bones. Later, I found out that I had six spinal fractures, three broken ribs, and a damaged lung.

The sight of people using e-cigarettes has become normal, but it's possible that their popularity may have already reached its peak. Most people who use e-cigarettes are smokers or recent ex-smokers, and statistics suggest that their numbers may be decreasing.

In 2014, a health charity called Action on Smoking and Health (ASH) reported that the number of adults in Britain using e-cigarettes had tripled since 2012 to 2.1 million. However, more recent figures from the Smoking Toolkit Study show that the growth in vaping has slowed down. In 2013, 22% of smokers and ex-smokers were using e-cigarettes, but this number dropped to 19% by the end of 2014.

Professor Robert West, who analyzes the data for the study, says that the decline is significant. He notes that most people who use e-cigarettes are smokers, and only a small percentage of non-smokers have tried them. "The numbers of people using e-cigarettes while still smoking are going down," he said. "We're not seeing growth in the number of long-term ex-smokers or non-smokers using e-cigarettes."

In contrast to the UK, vaping appears to be growing in popularity in the US. However, West questions the accuracy of the US data, which doesn't distinguish between people who have tried e-cigarettes once and those who use them regularly.

Experts say that fears about e-cigarettes becoming popular among young non-smokers are unfounded. Only 1.8% of children are regular users, according to ASH. Instead, e-cigarettes seem to be most popular among adults trying to quit smoking.

Scarlett Johansson is suing French author Grégoire Delacourt for €50,000 in damages. She claims his novel makes false statements about her personal life. The book, "The First Thing We Look At", tells the story of a French model who looks like Johansson. In the story, men see the model as only a sex object and women are jealous of her. The model has many adventures pretending to be Johansson until she is discovered and eventually dies in a car crash.

Johansson's lawyer says Delacourt's novel is a "violation" of her name, reputation, and image. He claims the book contains false statements about her private life and wants to stop it from being translated or made into a movie. The court case started in Paris, but neither Johansson nor Delacourt was there.

Delacourt says he chose to write about Johansson because she is "the archetype of beauty today". He insists that his character is not actually Johansson, but rather a fictional person who looks like her. Delacourt has become a well-known author in France, and his previous book was translated into 47 languages.

Delacourt thinks it's "sad" that Johansson is suing him. He says he wrote a love story and a tribute to feminine beauty, not a novel about a celebrity. He believes that if authors can't mention real people or things in their writing, it will be hard to create fiction.

Young Cubans are rushing to use a new free internet service in Havana, the capital city of Cuba. This service has been made possible by Kcho, one of Cuba's most famous artists. The cultural centre where Kcho works now offers free wi-fi, which is rare in Cuba. 

The state-owned telecommunications company, Etecsa, has approved this move. However, the internet connection can be very slow when many people are using it at the same time. In a country where only about 5% of the population has full access to the internet, this free service is seen as a big opportunity.

People can now use international news websites, talk to friends and family abroad, and visit social media sites like Facebook and Twitter. Adonis Ortiz, a 20-year-old user, said, "I come here as often as I can." He uses the internet to video-chat with his father in the US, whom he hasn't seen in nine years.

As relations between the US and Cuba improve, American tech companies like Google and Apple may soon enter the Cuban market. Meanwhile, Cuba has installed a high-speed internet cable from Venezuela and is using some Chinese equipment.

About 25% of Cubans have access to a restricted version of the internet, which only includes certain websites and limited email. Kcho's free wi-fi service is different because it gives users full access to the internet.

Kcho, whose real name is Alexis Leiva Machado, has close ties to the Cuban government. He announced that his actions had been approved by the Ministry of Culture. Kcho wants to encourage Cubans to learn about the internet and its benefits.

Scott Kelly spent 340 days on the International Space Station (ISS) with Russian astronaut Mikhail Kornienko. They were studying how space travel affects humans. This is important research for future missions to Mars. Kelly said the hardest part was being in space for so long. He felt sore when he returned to Earth, more than after shorter trips.

Kelly and his twin brother Mark have been taking physical and mental tests. These tests will help NASA learn about how our bodies cope with space travel. Kelly had aches and sensitive skin, but his balance is mostly okay. However, he struggled with gravity at first. He said it's easy to underestimate its effects.

When Kelly landed back on Earth, he was amazed by the fresh air and the smell of the spacecraft. He described the ISS as "a million pounds, the size of a football field" and said it uses solar power. The station is an international project that has been in space for 15 years.

Kelly took many photos of the Earth from space and posted them on social media. He said the planet looks beautiful but fragile. He could see pollution clouds and smoke from wildfires. Kelly believes we need to take care of our environment, especially the thin atmosphere that protects us.

During his time in space, Kelly kept himself busy with work and milestones like spacewalks and science experiments. He also followed news on Earth, including the presidential election. However, as a government employee, he couldn't comment on politics.

Kelly said being back on Earth feels strange, and he expects to experience culture shock soon. Although he might not fly with NASA again, he's open to working with private space companies like SpaceX in the future. He thinks that one day people will be able to buy tickets

Junior Smart knows a lot about gangs because he used to be part of one. When his mother died in his late teens, he joined a gang in south London. At first, it was fun, but soon it became more serious and involved making money through crime. He failed his GCSEs at school, but later passed them at college and got a job in administration. However, he also worked as a DJ and made extra money by selling drugs with the gang.

Eventually, Smart was arrested for serious drug-related crimes and sent to prison for 12 years. This experience changed him completely. "The first night after I was arrested was a huge wake-up call," he says. "I realized I had been living two separate lives." In prison, Smart saw how the system failed its inmates. He befriended a drug addict who kept returning to prison because his addiction wasn't treated.

This experience inspired Smart to start working as a "listener" in prison, helping new inmates adjust to life inside. After five years, he was released early and started his own project to help young people leave gangs. His team of 12 full-time workers and six volunteers work with the police and other organizations to support those trapped in violent gangs.

Smart believes that simply arresting gang leaders doesn't solve the problem. In fact, it can make things worse by creating a power vacuum that leads to more violence. He thinks that the government's approach is disjointed and that removing a leader can destabilize the entire gang. Instead of making the streets safer, it can create new conflicts and recruit more young people into gangs.

Gangs are now recruiting children as young as eight or nine years old, known as "tinies," to shield their seniors from risk.

Wales is set to become the first country in the UK where people are assumed to have agreed to donate their organs after death, unless they opt out. The Welsh Assembly voted 43-8 in favor of the new policy, with two abstentions.

The law will allow hospitals to assume that people who die want to donate their organs, unless they have specifically registered an objection. This change aims to increase organ donation and provide hope for the 226 people in Wales waiting for a transplant.

Welsh Health Minister Mark Drakeford said, "This is a huge day for Wales... As a society, we are prepared to take action to increase organ donation." He added that family refusal is a major factor affecting organ donations, often due to lack of knowledge about their loved one's wishes.

The new law will clarify people's wishes around organ donation and increase the rate of consent. Relatives or friends can still object to donation based on what they know about the deceased person's views.

Some opponents worry that the need for more organs could lead to overruling the wishes of those who have died and their families. However, ministers say there will be safeguards in place. Families will have a "clear right of objection" to show that the deceased would not have wanted to donate.

Wales has an acute shortage of organs, with about one person dying every week while on the waiting list. The government hopes the new law will encourage more people to become donors. Around a third of the Welsh population is already on the organ donor register, but many more say they are happy to donate in surveys.

John Lewis's 2015 Christmas advert tells the story of a lonely old man living on the moon and a young girl who tries to contact him. The department store is using its campaign to raise money for Age UK, a charity that helps elderly people who are alone during the holiday season.

The advert shows a young girl named Lily spotting the old man through her telescope and trying to send him messages. She eventually floats a present of a telescope tied to balloons up to the moon, allowing them to make contact. The strapline for the campaign is "Show someone they're loved this Christmas", which matches Age UK's own message: "No one should have no one at Christmas".

John Lewis has spent £7m on the campaign, including a TV advert, smartphone game, and merchandise such as glow-in-the-dark pyjamas. The retailer will also donate profits from three products to Age UK.

The advert was made with a budget of £1m and features music by Norwegian artist Aurora. It was filmed at Warner Bros Studios, where the Harry Potter films were made, and the set was designed by one of the team behind the latest Star Wars film.

John Lewis has been building interest in its campaign with a teaser on TV and social media using the hashtag #OnTheMoon. The retailer's head of marketing, Rachel Swift, said that the charity resonates with people at this time of year and that the advert encourages viewers to think about someone who might be alone during Christmas.

Europe is set to become the first region in the world to introduce 'real-world' emissions tests for car manufacturers, marking a significant step forward in the fight against air pollution. The new regulations will require cars to undergo emissions testing on real roads and in traffic conditions, rather than just in laboratory settings.

The European Commission has approved the plan, which aims to enforce a limit of 80mg of nitrogen oxide per kilometre. However, research suggests that only one in 16 cars currently meets this standard. Other countries, such as China and Korea, are also considering introducing similar real-world emissions tests and will be closely watching the EU's progress.

Air pollution from diesel engines is estimated to cause at least a quarter of the 29,000 annual deaths related to air pollution in the UK alone. The current laboratory test for measuring emissions has been criticized for being outdated and open to manipulation by car manufacturers. Studies have shown that lab results can be easily influenced by factors such as smooth roads, high temperatures, and even taping up doors and windows.

The European Commission is finalizing a proposal to introduce a new emissions testing procedure that will allow for more accurate assessments of vehicles in real driving conditions. The proposal still needs approval from other commissioners and a technical committee, but it is expected to pass without major hurdles.

Campaigners have welcomed the move, saying that car manufacturers have been cheating current tests by using tricks such as programming vehicles to enter low-emissions mode during lab experiments. "The development of a new, real-world driving emission test is an important step forward in tackling urban air pollution," said Greg Archer, clean vehicles manager for Transport and Environment.

Research has shown that actual nitrogen oxide emissions from cars are seven times higher than the 80mg/km standard

Lima has a problem with trash, but it's getting help from an unexpected source: black vultures. These birds are often seen as pests, but they're being used to fight against fly-tipping and illegal dumping. The environmental authorities have given ten of these birds special cameras and GPS trackers to find and record the locations of secret dumps.

One of these birds is Samuel, a Coragyps atratus who has been trained to sniff out rubbish. His trainer, Alfredo Correa, says that vultures are perfect for this job because they can eat dead animals without getting sick. They have strong stomachs that protect them from viruses and bacteria.

The project is a collaboration between the US Agency for International Development (USAID) and the Peruvian Environment Ministry. The goal is to tackle Lima's rubbish problem, which is serious: with only four landfills in a city of nearly ten million people, many residents dump their trash illegally. This contaminates the city's water sources, including the Rimac river.

The project has given the vultures names like Capitan Huggin and Capitana Aella. A video shows them flying over the city, with a dramatic voiceover that says they're fighting against disease and pestilence while humans ignore the danger. But the project is serious: it wants to encourage citizens to report fly-tipping and reduce their own waste.

The problem of trash in Lima is partly due to unpaid taxes. Many residents don't pay, which means some municipalities lack the resources for basic services like rubbish collection. The project shares the vultures' GPS coordinates with the municipalities, but it's up to them to collect the trash and change the habits of their residents.

Up to a billion people will still be extremely poor by 2030 unless countries focus on reducing inequalities and address social, economic, and cultural barriers that prevent them from escaping poverty. A new report by the Chronic Poverty Advisory Network (CPAN) warns that many people who rise above the poverty line of $1.25 a day may fall back into poverty due to shocks such as drought, illness, or conflict.

The report found that in some areas, up to 60% of people who escaped poverty fell back into it. Even in successful countries like Indonesia and Vietnam, around 20% of people who escaped poverty returned to it. The report highlights individual cases where people have slipped back into poverty due to personal setbacks or bigger crises.

Andrew Shepherd, a research fellow at the Overseas Development Institute, said: "We need to ensure that people lifted out of poverty remain above the poverty line permanently. Too many families are experiencing 'two steps forward, one step back', where they struggle to recover from personal or bigger setbacks."

The report argues that progress in reducing extreme poverty will be much harder in the next 15 years. Despite a drop in extreme poverty from 1.9 billion in 1990 to 1.2 billion in 2010, climate-related shocks and deep poverty in parts of sub-Saharan Africa will slow momentum.

To address this, the report calls for a shift in thinking about poverty to focus on the chronically poor – those who are poor for many years or their entire lives. It emphasizes the need to stop impoverishment and provide support to those living in chronic poverty.

Johanna Basford's colouring books for adults are currently the bestsellers on Amazon in the US. Her book "Secret Garden" has sold 1.4 million copies worldwide, while her new book "Enchanted Forest" has already sold nearly 226,000 copies. Many famous people, including Zooey Deschanel and Kim Ki-Bum, have shared pictures of Basford's books on social media.

The success of Basford's books is not an isolated case. Other colouring books for adults are also selling very well in the UK. Richard Merritt's "Art Therapy Colouring Book" and Millie Marotta's "Animal Kingdom" are among the top ten bestsellers on Amazon.co.uk, along with two more of Basford's titles.

Ana McLaughlin from Michael O'Mara Books says that colouring books have been reimagined as a way for adults to unwind and reduce stress. Basford believes that people enjoy her books because they offer a creative outlet without requiring any artistic talent. She also thinks that the nostalgia factor plays a role, as many adults used to colour when they were children. Now, colouring is socially acceptable and has become its own category of books for adults.

Margaret Allen's exercise class is a bit different from others. Halfway through, she lets her students have a tea break with cake and a sit down. This might seem unusual, but it works for Margaret and her eight students, who are all women in their 60s, 70s, and 80s.

Margaret, who is 93 years old, leads the class despite having some health problems. She has a trapped nerve in one leg and needs a new knee, but she doesn't let that stop her. In fact, she looks like she could keep going for hours.

During the tea break, Margaret's students chat about their lives and share stories. They also talk about how much they appreciate Margaret's class, which has been running for 45 years in the seaside town of Saltburn-by-the-Sea near Middlesbrough.

Margaret started leading exercise classes during World War II, when she played the piano for a keep-fit group. She took over as instructor in her 40s and has been doing it ever since. Her class used to have more than 18 regular students, but now there are only eight.

Despite their age, Margaret's students are very active. They do Scottish dances and other exercises that require a lot of energy. One student, Jean Cunion, says the group helped her through a difficult time when her mother died. Another student, Ruth Steere, is impressed by Margaret's ability to lead the class without even looking at them.

It started when a luxury hotel chain, Hankyu-Hanshin, admitted lying about where its ingredients came from on menus at some of its restaurants between 2006 and October 2013. This affected around 78,000 customers. 
One example was a dish described as "red salmon caviar" that actually contained flying fish eggs. The hotel group's president tried to apologize by cutting his own pay by 20% and other executives' pay by 10%, but this didn't calm angry customers down. 
The president later resigned, saying the company had "betrayed our customers", although he claimed they never meant to deceive them. One of the head chefs also turned down a medal from the government. 
So far, the company has given refunds to over 10,000 customers, totaling around 20 million yen. The total cost is expected to reach 110 million yen. 

This scandal has spread to other well-known hotels and restaurants in Japan. Although no one has gotten sick from eating mislabeled food, many consumers are still angry. For example, some people thought they were eating expensive kuruma shrimps, but actually got cheaper black tiger shrimps instead.

The first incident happened when a customer complained that a "scallop" dish at the Prince Hotel in Tokyo was not what it seemed. The hotel investigated and corrected over 50 menu items at its restaurants. This led other hotels to admit they had also misled customers about their ingredients.
