Author Philip Pullman says that downloading music or books without paying for them is a form of theft. He believes that people who do this are taking something that doesn't belong to them, just like stealing someone's wallet. Pullman, who is also president of the Society of Authors, thinks that copyright laws should be respected.

In an article, he writes that many internet users don't see anything wrong with downloading music or books for free. However, he argues that this is unfair to artists and writers who work hard to create their work. He says that these people often struggle financially and then have their chance of making a living taken away from them when others steal their work.

Pullman's article comes after music industry leaders met with British Prime Minister David Cameron to discuss web piracy. The issue of copyright is a contentious one, with some arguing that current laws are outdated and don't work in the digital age.

Cathy Casserly, chief executive of Creative Commons, disagrees with Pullman. She thinks that copyright laws should be changed to allow people to share and build on each other's work more easily. The debate about copyright is ongoing, and the scale of illegal downloading is significant. According to data from Ofcom, between November 2012 and January 2013, millions of music tracks, TV shows, films, ebooks, and software files were pirated in the UK. About 20 years ago, Larry Pizzi, an experienced executive in the bicycle industry, heard about electric bikes for the first time. He wondered why anyone would want to add a motor and batteries to a bike. This question still puzzles many traditionalists today.

Bicycle shops have been slow to sell e-bikes, even though they've been around since the late 1990s. Sales in the US have been modest so far. However, Pizzi, who is now CEO of Currie Technologies, the top seller of e-bikes in the US, believes that's about to change.

Well-known brands like Trek, Raleigh, and Specialized are now offering electric models, betting that the market will soon take off. "We're on the verge of mainstream adoption," Pizzi said. More companies are entering the market every month.

The US is different from other countries when it comes to e-bikes. In 2014, nearly 32 million e-bikes were sold worldwide, mostly in China, where they're used for transportation. They're also popular in Europe, especially in the Netherlands and Switzerland.

E-bikes are not like motorcycles or mopeds, which rely on motor power. Instead, they're bicycles that can be pedaled with or without help from an electric motor. Riding an e-bike feels like riding a regular bike with a strong tailwind. The motor helps you go faster or climb hills, but it's not the main source of power.

Is this the moment when music streaming becomes popular worldwide? 
In 2014, only 41 million people globally used music streaming services, according to the International Federation of the Phonographic Industry (IFPI). Although streaming is a growing area for the record business, it's still not widely used. Many subscribers got their service as part of a deal with their mobile phone operator, so it's unclear how many are actually using it. Apple has a talent for making existing products appealing to a wider audience. Recently leaked information suggests that Apple aims to reach 100 million subscribers, which would generate $12 billion annually. To put this in perspective, the global recorded music industry was worth just under $15 billion in 2014.

Is downloading coming to an end? 
The iTunes Store launched in 2003 and quickly became a huge success, with Apple dominating the market with around 70% share. Downloads still make up most of the digital income for recorded music, but revenue peaked in 2013 in the UK and fell in 2014. Apple bought Beats in 2014 to move from music ownership (downloads) to music access (subscription streaming). However, Apple can't abandon downloads yet, so both will coexist under the Apple brand.

Apple previously tried to create an artist-friendly platform called Ping, but it failed. Apple Connect is different, allowing artists to post music, videos, and photos on their profile pages. Apple has generally had good relations with the music industry and artists, treating music as "art" rather than "content". In contrast, Spotify has been criticized by artists like Thom Yorke and Taylor Swift.

When talking about climate change, people often focus on the problem but forget to think about the many possible solutions. These solutions include speeding up recycling, reducing emissions, and finding sustainable alternatives to things like plastic, air conditioning, smartphones, and fast fashion.

Recently, a group of experts met in Copenhagen to discuss their latest report on climate change. They found that climate change is happening all over the world and we need to work harder to reduce emissions before it gets out of control. The meeting also focused on solutions to these problems.

The Sustainia Award, led by Arnold Schwarzenegger, celebrated 10 innovative sustainability projects from around the world. These projects showed how people can make a difference in areas like food, fashion, energy, transportation, education, and health. They offered a positive alternative to the usual gloomy predictions about the future.

Some of these projects included producing plastic from greenhouse gases in California, recycling old clothes and shoes in Switzerland, and using smartphones to make bike-sharing easier in Canada. But one project stood out - Wecyclers from Nigeria.

Wecyclers helps low-income communities in Lagos earn money by collecting and recycling waste. They use bicycles to collect trash and then exchange it for goods like food or household items through a text message system. The recycled materials are turned into products like mattresses, pillows, and trash bags. This project is especially important because only 40% of the city's rubbish is currently collected.

Solutions to climate change don't always have to be high-tech or expensive. Sometimes simple ideas can make a big difference in people's lives. Sustainability is not just about reducing emissions; it's also about using natural resources wisely and creating healthier communities.

Riley B King was born near Itta Bena, Mississippi. Growing up, he had limited opportunities as an African-American farm worker. However, he learned guitar from a family friend and sang with a gospel group. In his early 20s, he moved to Memphis, where he played music regularly at a bar in West Memphis, Arkansas. He also worked as a disc jockey on a local radio station.

King started recording music in 1949, but it wasn't until 1952 that he had his first hit with "Three O'Clock Blues." This song was the start of many successes, including "Please Love Me" and "Sweet Sixteen." King's style was innovative and rooted in blues history. He often praised musicians who influenced him, such as T-Bone Walker.

King developed his guitar technique because he couldn't play in a certain style. He also sang in a unique way, blending different styles together. His favorite composer and singer was Louis Jordan, whom he honored with an album in 1999.

In the 1950s, King played at many black-patronized theaters and clubs. In 1962, he signed with a major record label, but his first records didn't do well. However, his live album "Live at the Regal" (1965) became iconic and helped him gain popularity among younger musicians.

Kenton Cool's voice is barely above a whisper after climbing at high altitude. He has just flown down from Everest base camp to Kathmandu, Nepal's capital city. Over the previous weekend, he completed an impressive series of climbs. On Saturday morning, he reached the summit of Nuptse, the first and lowest peak in the Everest "horseshoe". Later that day, he climbed to the top of Everest itself, reaching the summit in complete darkness early on Sunday. Then, on Monday morning, he and his partner climbed Lhotse, the third peak in this challenging three-summit climb.

Cool says it was a rare opportunity because all three mountains had fixed ropes for the first time since the late 1990s. However, he believes that future climbers will set new standards by climbing without ropes or bottled oxygen. Sixty years after Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay first climbed Everest, Cool looks to the future of mountaineering.

He mentions Swiss climber Ueli Steck, who had planned to climb Everest's west ridge without fixed ropes before descending to the South Col and then climbing Lhotse via a new route. However, Steck left the mountain after an altercation with Sherpas at Camp 2. Cool praises Steck as a technically brilliant climber who had taken his physical condition to an extremely high level.

A new international survey across 33 countries shows that people have many misconceptions about social realities. 

For example, British people think the top 1% of households own 59% of their country's wealth, but they actually own only 23%. Americans believe 33% of their population are immigrants, when in fact it is only 14%. Brazilians think the average age in their country is 56, but it is actually 31. Russians think that 31% of their politicians are women, when it is only 14%.

In Britain, people think 43% of young adults aged 25-34 still live at home with their parents, but the actual number is 14%. In India, online users believe 60% of the whole country has internet access, when in fact only 19% do.

Why are people so often wrong about these realities? One reason is that we struggle with basic math and sometimes misunderstand questions. For example, most countries greatly overestimate how many people do not follow a religion: respondents said 37%, but the actual number is just 18%. This may be because people think of those who practice their religion rather than what they put on census forms.

People also take mental shortcuts, using easily available information even if it doesn't quite fit the question. Our overestimates of rural populations are often based on how much land rural areas cover, not how many people actually live there. This is an example of "fast" thinking, rather than careful consideration.

Scientists warn that many animals are in danger of disappearing forever. This is not just about well-known animals like tigers, orangutans, and pandas. The real problem is with smaller creatures like ladybirds, which play a crucial role in keeping our environment healthy.

Climate change, pollution, and the growing human population are causing many species to disappear at an alarming rate. Some scientists believe we have entered a new geological age called the Anthropocene, where humans are having a devastating impact on the planet.

A report by the World Wildlife Fund (WWF) found that between 1970 and 2014, the number of vertebrates (animals with backbones) decreased by 52%. Freshwater species declined by 76% during the same period. This loss of biodiversity has reached critical levels.

However, it's not just the big animals that are important. Smaller creatures like bees, hoverflies, and worms provide essential services to our ecosystem. Without them, our food production would be severely affected. For example, three-quarters of the world's food production relies on pollinators like bees.

Dr Nick Isaac, a scientist at the Centre for Ecology & Hydrology, says that the decline of common species will have a bigger impact on humans than the loss of rare creatures. He notes that Britain's insects and invertebrates are declining just as fast as vertebrates, with serious consequences for humanity.

The main cause of this problem is unsustainable human consumption, which damages ecosystems, creates climate change, and destroys habitats at an alarming rate. The WWF warns that if we don't take action, the consequences will be severe.

Costa's appointment was met with surprise and some skepticism, but many people welcomed the decision. Véronique Soulier, president of the club's supporters' association, said, "As a woman, it makes me happy. We all agree that having a woman in charge is no bad thing."

Britain has been found to be the loneliest country in Europe by the Office for National Statistics. British people are less likely to have close friends or know their neighbours than anyone else in the EU, and many have no one to turn to in a crisis. Research has shown that loneliness is twice as bad for older people's health as obesity and can be almost as deadly as poverty.

However, younger adults are also struggling with loneliness. A 2010 study by the Mental Health Foundation found that young people were more likely to feel lonely often, worry about feeling alone, and feel depressed because of loneliness than older people. This is a problem because loneliness is closely linked to mental health issues such as stress, depression, anxiety, and addiction.

There are few services available to help young people with loneliness, as most support is focused on the elderly. Sam Challis from the charity Mind says that when young people turn 21, they're too old for youth services but may not have developed strong social connections yet.

So, what can young people do to combat loneliness? While social media and the internet can be helpful in connecting with others, they can also make us feel more isolated if we compare our lives to others. Dr Grant Blank from the Oxford Internet Institute suggests that using technology to meet new people can be beneficial, but it's not a replacement for face-to-face contact.

Meditation techniques and apps may not be the best solution for loneliness either, as they encourage solo reflection. Instead, addressing the underlying causes of loneliness is key. For example, if you're struggling to leave the house, using online communities or helplines can provide support.

A new computer-assisted autopsy system called 'Virtopsy' is being used in some European hospitals. Its inventor claims that this technique could eventually make it impossible to commit a 'perfect murder'. 

The Virtopsy method was developed by scientists at the University of Zurich and is now used in several forensic medical institutes in Europe. Instead of making an incision in the body, pathologists can examine the corpse in 3D on computer screens.

Michael Thali, one of the inventors of Virtopsy, says it has the potential to revolutionize criminal investigations. "With a virtual autopsy, you can find every piece of evidence," he said. This means that there will be no such thing as a 'perfect murder' anymore.

Virtopsies use images from MRI and CT scans, as well as surface scans of dead bodies. These devices are combined to create a 'Virtobot'. The technique allows doctors to detect injuries that may not be visible during a traditional autopsy, such as internal bleeding or cancer.

Richard Dirndorfer, one of the pioneers of DNA analysis in criminology and a founder developer of Virtopsy, believes that the method could eventually replace traditional autopsies. "I think it will happen gradually," he said.

The computer imaging techniques allow doctors to gain detailed insights into the body without making an incision. The method has already helped discover injuries that were not detected during conventional autopsies.

Forensic scientists can use Virtopsy to plan their autopsies more efficiently, according to Dominic Wichmann, an internal medicine specialist at Hamburg's University Hospital. Criminologists from around the world have been visiting Switzerland to learn about the new method.

In Iceland, you can have many unusual names like Aagot, Arney, or Ásfríður. But there's one name you cannot have: Harriet. Tristan Cardew and his Icelandic wife Kristin are fighting against a decision by the National Registry in Reykjavik. The registry won't renew their 10-year-old daughter Harriet's passport because it doesn't recognize her first name.

The registry also doesn't recognize the name of Harriet's 12-year-old brother Duncan. Until now, they have travelled on passports that just say "Girl" and "Boy" Cardew. But this time, the authorities are following the rules strictly. The law says that no official document can be issued to people with unapproved Icelandic names.

The family was in trouble because they might miss their holiday in France. They had to apply for an emergency UK passport from the British embassy. In Iceland, a country with only 320,000 people, names are very important. Most surnames just mean "son of" or "daughter of". For example, Jón Einarsson's children might be Ólafur Jónsson and Sigríður Jónsdóttir.

The law says that parents must submit their child's name to the National Registry within six months of birth. If the name is not on a list of approved names, the parents need to get permission from the Icelandic Naming Committee. The committee gets about 100 applications every year and rejects half of them. Google has mapped many parts of the world, including the highest mountains, the ocean floor, and the Amazon rainforest. However, it had not fully explored the Arctic region until now. The company is working on a significant update to its maps of the polar areas, which will help people understand life in these regions better.

A team from Google traveled to Iqaluit, the largest town in the Canadian territory of Nunavut, with warm clothing, laptops, and a special camera. They were helped by an Inuit mapping expert and spent four days collecting images and information about the town. The goal is to add Iqaluit to Google's Street View application, which will allow people around the world to explore the town online.

The team had to hike through snow-covered roads and trails, some of which are made of ice and disappear in the summer. They also mapped a 15km road that is not well-known, despite warnings about polar bears and other wildlife. The locals were excited about the project and followed the team as they worked.

Iqaluit has a population of around 7,000 people and will be available on Street View in July 2013. The town's mayor, John Graham, said that this project is important because it will help people understand the town better. He also mentioned that Iqaluit was founded after an English explorer visited the area in 1576.

One of the challenges Google faced was gathering accurate data about the town. They had to correct mistakes and add new information, such as roads that were built recently. The team also worked with local residents to ensure that businesses and homes were correctly located on the map.

In Italy's Sardinia region, the mayor of Elmas, Valter Piscedda, has come up with an unusual solution. He wants to pay ten unemployed residents to leave the town and look for work elsewhere in Europe.

There are two main natural factors that can cause a city to slowly fall apart or even disappear: water and sand. If the Earth were getting colder instead of hotter, we could also add ice to this list. A rare "ice tsunami" in 2013 showed how powerful ice can be when it destroyed homes in Ochre Beach, Canada.

However, most cities are not threatened by ice. Instead, they are vulnerable because of rising sea levels caused by melting ice. Venice, Italy is a good example. A century ago, the city flooded about ten times a year, but now its lowest point floods around 100 times a year. The problem is not just the rising sea level, but also the fact that the land itself is sinking.

Venice's soil has compacted due to industrial activities, causing it to sink by 20cm between 1950 and 1970. Ho Chi Minh City in Vietnam is also sinking at a rate of about 2cm per year. Jakarta, Indonesia is sinking even faster, at a rate of 10-20cm per year. This has caused the city's seawall to become less effective.

Miami, Florida is another city that is struggling with rising sea levels and flooding. The city is built on porous limestone, which absorbs water from the sea. This causes sewage to rise up through drains and pipes, polluting the fresh water supply. If nothing is done, Miami may one day become uninhabitable.

Many young adults are staying with their parents for longer due to the housing crisis. A recent survey found that one in five young adults stay at home until they are at least 26, and the same proportion don't pay any rent. The number of adults living at home varies across the country, from 9% in the East Midlands to over 18% in London, where house prices and rents are highest.

Low wages and high rents are making it difficult for young adults to save money. Research by the homeless charity Shelter found that half of tenants can't save any money towards a deposit, while a quarter can only save £100 or less per month. Although mortgages are cheaper due to low interest rates, borrowers need large deposits to get the best deals.

As a result, many young adults are returning to their family home to save money. The survey found that 28% of adults live at home because they're trying to save for a deposit. In the 1970s, Bowie led the way in music trends and pop fashion. He started as a mime and cabaret performer in the late 1960s but soon became a singer-songwriter and pioneer of glam-rock. Ethiopia is one of the world’s poorest countries with serious food security problems. But it's also where teff comes from - a nutritious ancient grain that's becoming popular in health-food shops and supermarkets in Europe and America.

In Ethiopia, teff is very important. About 6.3 million farmers grow it, covering over 20% of all cultivated land. The grain is used to make injera, a fermented flatbread that's central to Ethiopian cuisine and many cultural ceremonies. 

Outside of Ethiopian communities abroad, teff was largely unknown for decades. But with the growing demand for traditional crops and gluten-free foods, teff is gaining popularity. It's even being called Ethiopia’s “second gift to the world”, after coffee.

Sophie Kebede, a London-based entrepreneur who sells teff products in the UK, says she was amazed by its nutritional value. "I didn't know it was so sought after. I'm of Ethiopian origin and have been eating injera all my life."

The Ice Bucket Challenge has raised $100m for a US charity and £4.5m for a British one, as well as thousands more for charities in Hong Kong and Australia. However, some people have criticized the challenge. They say that celebrities are showing off their bodies, people are having fun without donating, and water is being wasted.

The US Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) Association has also been criticized for paying its top staff high salaries. The association tried to patent the phrase "Ice Bucket Challenge", but withdrew its application after criticism.

The challenge started in the US in July and involves people pouring a bucket of ice water over their heads or nominating others to do so, while donating to charity. Some celebrities, including David Cameron and Pamela Anderson, have refused to take part.

Pamela Anderson wrote an open letter to the ALS Association saying she couldn't support its record on animal experimentation. Some US stars rejected the challenge because of California's drought. Others found alternative ways to participate, such as using recycled water or milk.

The challenge has been blamed for causing a water shortage on a Scottish island and some people have criticized it for being wasteful. However, charities say that the awareness and donations generated by the challenge are invaluable.

The Motor Neurone Disease (MND) Association in Britain says that the challenge has brought in a huge amount of money and attention to the disease. The charity's fundraising director said that they didn't expect the challenge to take off, but are grateful for the windfall.

The MND Association uses donations to fund research into the causes of the disease and to provide care and support for people affected by it. They say that every penny counts and will be used to make a difference

Scientists have designed a special mirror that can send heat into space and cool down buildings. This could replace traditional air-conditioning units and save energy. In the US, about 15% of the energy used by buildings goes to air conditioning. Researchers think their mirror could reduce this amount significantly.

The mirror was tested on a rooftop in Stanford, California. It stayed up to 5°C cooler than the surrounding air temperature, even when other surfaces were much hotter. According to Shanhui Fan, who led the development of the mirror, "If you cover a significant part of the roof with this mirror, you can see how much power it can save."

Buildings get warm from various sources, including hot water boilers, cooking facilities, and sunlight. The Stanford mirror reflects 97% of visible light and works as a thermal radiator, releasing heat into space at a specific wavelength. This makes it an effective way to cool down buildings.

The mirror is made up of several thin layers, including reflective silver and silicon dioxide. When heated, the silicon dioxide radiates heat as infrared light that passes through the atmosphere and into space. The total thickness of the mirror is about two micrometres.

In tests, the mirror had a cooling power of 40 watts per square metre at ambient temperature. According to Fan, installing the mirrors could cost between $20 and $70 per square metre and save around 100MWh of electricity per year on a three-storey building.

The mirror can cool buildings by being in direct contact with them or by cooling water that is then pumped around the building. However, it's unlikely to be used as a solution to slow down global warming, as it would only cover a small portion of the Earth's surface.

A new invention could bring light to millions of people in Africa and India without using expensive or dangerous fuels. The "gravity light" is powered by gravity, not batteries or electricity. It was invented by British designer Patrick Hunt.

Hunt had trouble getting funding for his project from banks and investors. They thought it was too risky. So he tried crowdfunding on a website called Indiegogo. He raised £36,200 in just five days and eventually got £400,000 in 40 days.

The light works by using a weight to generate power as it falls. The weight is lifted up and then allowed to fall slowly, creating enough energy for half an hour of light. Hunt plans to start producing the lights in China and will test them in Africa before making millions more.

Hunt is one of many entrepreneurs using crowdfunding to raise money for their projects. Indiegogo is a popular website that allows people to donate money to projects they like. In return, donors can get rewards or "perks," such as one of the gravity lights.

Danae Ringelmann, co-founder of Indiegogo, says that crowdfunding is a fair and efficient way for entrepreneurs to raise money. It's not about who you know or how much money you have, but about how good your idea is. She started Indiegogo in 2008 to help artists and filmmakers raise money.

Today, Indiegogo raises around $2 million per week for new businesses. The website has launched campaigns in euros and pounds and is popular in the UK. Ringelmann says that Indiegogo is different from other crowdfunding websites because it allows anyone to start a campaign, no matter how unusual their idea is.

JMW Turner, one of Britain's greatest painters, will be featured on the new £20 note. This decision was made after a nationwide vote where people chose a deceased cultural figure they thought deserved this great honour.

Turner is famous for his dramatic paintings of the sea. He beat 590 other artists, designers, and celebrities who were suggested by 30,000 members of the public. The list included well-known names like Alfred Hitchcock and Alexander McQueen.

A panel of experts chose the final five candidates based on their contribution to art and British society. Turner was chosen along with four others: Barbara Hepworth, Charlie Chaplin, Josiah Wedgwood, and William Hogarth.

The announcement was made at the Turner Contemporary gallery in Margate, a town where Turner often visited. The Bank of England governor, Mark Carney, and artist Tracey Emin made the announcement together.

Carney said it was important to involve the public in this decision. He believes that banknotes can be more than just practical - they can also be works of art. "Money is memory for a country and its people," he said. "Banknotes celebrate our heritage, culture, and achievements."

Turner's self-portrait from 1799 will feature on the new note, along with his famous painting The Fighting Temeraire. A quote from Turner - "light is therefore colour" - and his signature will also be included.

The new £20 note will replace the one featuring Adam Smith and will enter circulation by 2020. This is the first time the public has had a say in whose face appears on a British banknote.

Researchers from Britain and the Netherlands have made a breakthrough by developing a new method that can detect lies with an accuracy rate of over 70%. This method could be used in police stations worldwide within a decade. Instead of looking for facial expressions or body language like waving arms, the new method uses a full-body motion suit to track movements.

The polygraph is widely used in the US but has been met with skepticism by scientists and lawyers due to its reliability issues. In contrast, the new method has performed well in experiments. The idea behind it is that people who lie tend to fidget more, which can be detected using a special suit with 17 sensors.

He said, "Decades of research show that interviewers can only slightly better than randomly guess whether someone is telling the truth or lying." The polygraph has been around since the 1920s and measures physiological stress caused by anxiety, but it's not very reliable.

Rebecka Singerer was tired of being told that certain beers were "too dark and too strong" for her. She wanted to show that women can drink whatever they want. So, she joined a group called FemAle in Gothenburg, Sweden. The group's goal is to make beer more accessible to women.

The group is fighting against decades of prejudice in the beer world. Big breweries have tried to sell beer to women by making lighter, sweeter beers, but these efforts have failed. FemAle's approach is different - they organize tastings where women can try different types of beer and learn more about them.

Despite being top of the opinion polls for four months, Trump expressed self-doubt. However, this feeling quickly passed, and he returned to his usual confident tone.

In 2010, the old city in Srinagar was a place where police only went wearing body armour. It was a stronghold for separatists who wanted an independent Kashmir, and there were violent uprisings that killed over 100 people. But things have changed quickly. Abdullah says this is frustrating, as it makes tourists' insurance invalid when they visit. The last time foreign tourists were murdered in J&K was in 1995, when six westerners were kidnapped by a militant group.

Abdullah argues that the UK allows people to visit countries where British citizens have been killed more recently. He says there is no reason to single out Jammu and Kashmir as an unsafe destination. Germany relaxed its guidelines for travellers to the region in 2011, advising that foreigners are generally not targets of clashes.

James Hamblin, an editor at The Atlantic magazine, decided to stop showering regularly as part of his series 'If Our Bodies Could Talk'. He wanted to see what happens when we clean our bodies too much. To do this, he reduced the number of showers he took and stopped using shampoo and soap. What he found out was that many people already know: when we try too hard to be clean, our skin works harder to balance itself, making us want to shower again.

When we shower, we strip our skin of its natural oils and good bacteria. This can make our skin feel tight and dry, like it's two sizes too small. Our skin is home to millions of helpful bacteria, just like our gut. But when we shower, these bacteria are washed away. When they grow back, they can produce smells that might make us stink more.

Hamblin discovered that when he stopped using soap and showering, his skin went through a rough period at first, but then it balanced out. His skin started producing the right amount of oil again, and good bacteria grew back. He realized that our bodies are actually quite healthy on their own.

Reducing how often we shower can also help the environment. The average shower uses 65 liters of clean water, which is wasted when we add soap to it. With many places facing droughts, like California, conserving water is becoming more important. Additionally, using fewer body wash products can reduce waste and pollution.

Moses King, a 48-year-old man from Liberia, has been living with HIV for many years. Despite having access to antiretroviral medication, he struggled to feed his family of six children. As a subsistence farmer, he grew vegetables and bought rice, but meat and fish were too expensive.

King's situation is not unique in Liberia, where 1.5% of the population lives with HIV. Many people with HIV struggle to access nutritious food, which is essential for their health. Pate K Chon, a counsellor who works with HIV sufferers, recognized this problem and came up with an innovative solution.

Chon had seen a documentary about fish farming in Thailand and thought it could work in Liberia. She believed that fish farming could provide a stable source of protein for people with HIV and also create jobs. With the help of John Sheehy, a philanthropist, Chon built a fish farm in Monrovia, Liberia's capital.

The Grow2Feed Liberia Fish Farm now has 12 tanks, which can produce up to 200,000 fish per year. The farm serves a community of 1,200 people, mostly HIV-positive, including King and his family. In addition to providing fish, the farm also uses waste from the tanks to irrigate crops, creating more food and income for the community.

The project has been successful in providing nutritious food and jobs for people with HIV. It has also helped to reduce stigma around the illness by giving people a way to engage with their communities. According to Chon, good nutrition is crucial for people with HIV, as it helps them to stay healthy and respond well to treatment.

For 85 years, Pluto was just a grey blob on maps of our solar system. But on July 15, we saw it in high resolution for the first time. The pictures showed dramatic mountain ranges made of solid water ice, similar to those found in the Alps or the Rockies.

The New Horizons spacecraft sent back these amazing images from 4 billion miles away. Alan Stern, who led the mission, said they were a "home run" for his team. "New Horizons is giving us incredible results already," he added. "The data looks fantastic, and Pluto and its moon Charon are just mind-blowing."

One of the biggest surprises was finding mountains in the Kuiper belt, a region of our solar system that's full of icy objects. John Spencer, a scientist on the mission, said these mountains are around 11,000 feet high and several hundred miles across.

The pictures also showed an edge of Pluto with no craters, suggesting that its surface has been recently changed by geological activity. This could include geysers blasting ice into the atmosphere or volcanoes erupting with ice instead of molten rock.

Scientists believe the mountains on Pluto are made of water ice with a thin layer of other ices like methane and nitrogen. They think these mountains formed no more than 100 million years ago, which is very recent in terms of our solar system's age.

The images also showed that Pluto's surface is smooth, suggesting that geological activity is still happening there. This could be due to internal heat or snowfalls covering the surface.

The New Horizons spacecraft took 16 months to send back all its data from the fly-by. The team also named a heart-shaped feature on Pluto after Clyde Tomba

Roger McKinlay, former president of the Royal Institute of Navigation, thinks that relying too much on GPS technology could harm our natural ability to navigate. He believes that if we don't use these skills, they will get worse as we rely more on smartphones and other devices.

McKinlay says that a lot of money needs to be invested in navigation systems before technologies like self-driving cars can become a reality. In the meantime, he thinks that children should learn traditional navigation skills, such as reading maps, in school.

According to Ofcom, 66% of adults in the UK owned a smartphone in 2015, making GPS technology widely available. However, McKinlay warns that we should be careful not to rely too much on our devices for navigation. He says that navigation is a skill that can be lost if it's not used.

Research from 2009 supports this idea. A study found that retired London taxi drivers performed worse in navigation tests than those who were still working. This suggests that our navigation skills can decline if we don't use them regularly.

Neuroscientist Dr Hugo Spiers agrees that relying too much on GPS technology can be a problem, but he thinks the biggest risk is that people might get into danger because they're not paying attention to their surroundings. There have been cases where people have gotten lost or had accidents because of satnavs.

Spiers also says that how we use navigation technology can affect its impact on our skills. For example, using a smartphone app as a digital map requires more thinking and interaction than just following audio instructions.

The electric vehicle has no pedals or steering wheel and can be controlled using a smartphone app. It has a single STOP button between the two front-facing seats in case of an emergency.

The car takes care of all navigation, steering, acceleration, and braking tasks on its own. Google is building around 100 prototypes for a two-year test. The company's co-founder, Sergey Brin, says the project aims to improve safety and help people who struggle with transportation.

Google plans to license its technology to traditional vehicle manufacturers once it has refined it. Valdevaqueros beach in southern Spain is one of the last untouched beaches in the area. The sky above its golden sand is filled with kitesurfers and windsurfers taking advantage of the strong winds. However, this peaceful scene may soon change. On May 29, the local council in Tarifa approved plans to build a large tourist complex next to the beach, featuring 1,400 hotel rooms and 350 apartments.

Environmental groups are strongly opposed to the project, arguing that it will harm the habitats of protected species. However, many councillors believe that the project is necessary to create jobs in a town where 2,600 people out of 18,000 inhabitants are unemployed. Spain is currently facing its worst economic crisis in decades, and tourism is seen as a way to boost the local economy.

The complex would be built 800 meters from the coast, which complies with environmental standards. However, opponents argue that it's not necessary to build more housing in an area where there are already many empty homes. They also point out that the project may harm the local ecosystem and reduce the strength of the famous Levant wind.

Surfers who regularly visit the beach are worried about the impact of the new buildings on their sport. "It's not a family-friendly spot," said Henning Mayer, a surfer from Germany. "The Levant wind is very strong, and I don't think traditional tourists will be interested in coming here."

Campaigners have launched a Facebook page to save the beach, with support from groups like Greenpeace and the World Wide Fund for Nature. They argue that the project would harm the local wildlife and destroy the natural beauty of the area.

Scientists have created a detailed map of the brain that shows how words and their meanings are organized across different areas. This "atlas of the brain" uses colors to display how individual words and concepts can be grouped together in clusters.

The goal was to build a comprehensive map that shows how language is represented in the brain, specifically the meanings of words. Jack Gallant, a neuroscientist at the University of California, Berkeley, led the study.

No single area of the brain holds one word or concept. Instead, each area is associated with multiple related words. When we think of a word, many different areas of the brain light up together to represent its meaning. These networks can include concepts like life and love, death and taxes, or clouds and Florida.

The atlas was created by recording people's brain activity while they listened to stories on the radio. The scientists then matched the transcripts with the brain activity data to show how groups of related words triggered responses in 50,000 to 80,000 tiny spots across the brain.

One potential use for this technology is a language decoder that could allow people who are unable to speak due to motor neuron disease or locked-in syndrome to communicate through a computer. The atlas also shows how words and related terms activate the same areas of the brain. For example, the word "victim" activates the same area as "killed", "convicted", and "murdered".

Each word is represented by multiple areas because words can have multiple meanings. The scientists created an interactive website where people can explore the brain atlas.

A Canadian man named Jordan Axani became famous after offering a free trip around the world to a woman with the same name as his ex-girlfriend. He went on the trip with Elizabeth Quinn Gallagher, but they didn't fall in love. Instead, they developed a close friendship like siblings.

Axani had booked the three-week vacation with his ex-girlfriend, but when they broke up, he couldn't change the name on the flights. So, he offered the ticket to any Canadian named Elizabeth Gallagher. Quinn, a 23-year-old student from Nova Scotia, replied to his post on Reddit and was chosen.

Before the trip, Quinn made it clear that she had a serious boyfriend, but people still hoped that Axani and Quinn might fall in love. However, Axani said that their relationship was never romantic and that they only became good friends. It took them about a week to get used to traveling together and figure each other out.

Axani described the trip as "fantastic" and said that his favorite place was Prague, where they met many people who were excited to meet them. The pair were followed by fans on Twitter and Instagram, and they even got recognized in the street in Hong Kong.

After returning to Toronto, Axani went straight into a meeting with his charity organization, A Ticket Forward, which he started after his Reddit post became popular. He plans to offer round-the-world trips to survivors of abuse, cancer, and war. Axani is also talking to production companies about turning his story into a TV show or film.

As for his love life, Axani said that he's not looking for anything right now. "Life happens, and we'll see," he said.

US researchers think a nasal spray containing the 'Love hormone' oxytocin could help children with autism deal better with social situations. They found that one dose of oxytocin improved brain responses to facial expressions in children with autistic spectrum disorder. This change could make social interactions feel more natural and enjoyable for them.

The scientists believe that using oxytocin with existing therapies could improve their effectiveness. These therapies teach people with autism how to cope with social situations. "Over time, we expect to see improvements in social behavior, such as being more interested in interacting with others, making eye contact, and having better conversations," said Kevin Pelphrey from Yale University.

Autism is a developmental disorder that affects over 1% of the population. It causes difficulties with social interaction and communication. Currently, there is no established treatment for these social problems. Researchers at Yale have been studying oxytocin as a potential treatment because it plays a crucial role in bonding and trust.

The researchers used brain scans to study how oxytocin affects the brains of 17 children with autism aged 8-16. They found that after inhaling oxytocin, the reward centers in their brains worked more normally when looking at faces, but not when viewing cars. This suggests that oxytocin could help people with autism find social interactions more enjoyable.

However, it's too early to use oxytocin as a treatment for autism. The researchers warn against buying oxytocin online and trying it at home. "We need more research before we can consider this a viable treatment," said Pelphrey. Other experts agree that while the study is promising, more research is needed to understand the benefits and risks of using oxytocin.

Cathal Redmond was taking photos with his first underwater camera off the Greek coast when he realized something was wrong. The colourful fish looked brown and murky in his pictures. He thought the problem was that he didn't have enough time to set up the shots while holding his breath. As an industrial designer, Redmond wanted to find a way to give people more time underwater.

Redmond invented the Express Dive, a device that lets users swim underwater for two minutes. It's like a cross between a scuba mouthpiece and a water bottle. The user holds it in their mouth, and it provides air from a refillable tank. This invention aims to fill the gap between snorkelling, which has limited time, and scuba diving, which requires expensive and cumbersome gear.

Redmond, 27, completed a scuba-diving course in 2006 and loved being able to breathe underwater. However, he didn't enjoy wearing all the heavy equipment like fins, weight belt, wetsuit, air tank, and mask. He felt limited by the gear and wanted to find a way to make it easier for people to explore underwater.

The Express Dive has two main parts. When above water, it uses a fan to suck in air, which is then compressed and stored in the tank. The device can hold enough air for two minutes of diving and takes about the same time to refill. A display light shows when the air is running low.

Redmond tested individual parts of the prototype, made from high-density foam, aluminium, and silicone. He showed that the motor can compress two minutes' worth of air into the unit, and the design can be held in the diver's mouth. However, he hasn't yet tested the device

The action comes as a Starbucks executive appears before a parliamentary committee to answer questions about why the company paid no corporation tax in the UK over the past three years, despite making large profits. The company's Chief Financial Officer will try to repair its reputation, which has been damaged by the controversy.

MPs have accused tax officials of being too close to big businesses and not doing enough to collect taxes owed. One MP said that the arrangement between Starbucks and tax officials "smells bad". UK Uncut is trying to link government cuts, particularly those affecting women, to tax avoidance by multinational companies.

The group says that if companies like Starbucks paid their fair share of tax, the government could fund vital services such as refuges for women and children. Tax officials estimate that £32 billion was lost to tax avoidance in 2011. UK Uncut has previously targeted other companies, including Vodafone and Topshop, over their tax payments.

Starbucks has been accused of paying only £8.6 million in corporation tax since it launched in the UK in 1998, despite making sales of £3 billion. The company insists that it pays the correct level of taxes and points out that it has paid over £160 million in other taxes, including National Insurance contributions and VAT.

The High Court rejected the government's argument that too much time had passed since the 1950s insurgency, making it impossible to hold a fair trial. In 2011, the same judge, Mr Justice McCombe, also rejected the claim that the Kenyan government should be sued instead of the British government.

Human rights activists in Kenya estimate that over 5,000 people who were detained by British colonial authorities are still alive and may bring claims against the UK government. The ruling could also allow victims of colonial atrocities in other parts of the world to sue.

The Foreign Office acknowledged that the ruling has significant implications and plans to appeal. They argue that the normal time limit for bringing a civil action is three to six years, but in this case, it has been extended to over 50 years.

The court victory was the result of a three-year battle by Paulo Muoka Nzili, Wambugu Wa Nyingi, and Jane Muthoni Mara. They suffered severe mistreatment, including castration, beatings, and sexual assaults. Two other claimants dropped out or died during the process.

In Nairobi, the news was met with joy by two of the complainants, who had been waiting anxiously for the decision. Nyingi said he wanted the truth to be known so that future generations could understand what happened. Mara expressed her happiness and relief, saying she would tell her children that she won.

Sleep used to be seen as a sign of laziness, but now it's considered essential for success. Arianna Huffington's book "The Sleep Revolution" has become a best-seller, and she's encouraging people to prioritize sleep to improve their lives. The sleep industry is booming, with luxury hotels offering "sleep retreats" and companies creating nap pods for employees.

But how did sleep become so fashionable? One reason is that it fits into the lifestyle of people who value health and wellness. With the rise of wearable technology, people are tracking their sleep patterns and trying to optimize them for better performance. Huffington argues that sleep is not just about resting, but also about restoring energy and improving productivity.

However, getting enough sleep is not just a matter of personal choice. It's also linked to socioeconomic factors. Studies have shown that people from lower-income backgrounds tend to sleep poorly due to stress, safety concerns, and irregular work schedules. There's also a racial gap in sleep quality, with African Americans sleeping less than white people.

In reality, the people who get the most sleep are wealthy white women - likely the same demographic targeted by Huffington's book. While she calls her promotion of sleep a "revolution," it's more like a rebranding of an existing issue. The real sleep crisis is not about rich people undervaluing sleep, but about the majority of people struggling to afford time for rest.

The military is already researching ways to reduce the need for sleep, with the goal of creating soldiers who can perform at their best on minimal rest. This could lead to a future where only the poor are forced to spend a third of their lives sleeping, while the wealthy have access to technology that allows them to function without rest.

After hiding for 14 months, Duran is not sorry about what he did. "I'm proud of what I did," he said in an interview from a secret location. He believes the money helped create opportunities and allowed people to build a network of alternative initiatives.

Duran took out loans by creating fake identities and companies. He used the money to fund social activists, speaking tours against capitalism, and equipment for a media network. He wanted to show that the banking system was unfair and created money out of thin air.

The banks eventually discovered what Duran had done and he was arrested in 2009. He spent two months in prison before being released on bail. In 2013, facing up to eight years in prison, he decided to flee rather than go to trial. "I don't think the justice system is fair," he said.

Today, Duran believes that his actions would be better understood in Spain, but they are no longer needed. The anti-capitalist movement has grown and is now supported by thousands of people.

Thousands of people are taking unnecessary treatments and following inadequate diets because of fake allergy tests. This can lead to malnutrition, especially in children. A group of experts and charities has warned about the dangers of these tests. They say that allergies and food intolerances are increasing, but many people are confused about what they mean.

Tracey Brown from Sense About Science said, "This is a big problem for science communication. Many people believe myths and misinformation about allergies." She added, "The consequences are serious – some people take unnecessary actions, while others don't get the help they need."

Experts are worried that restaurants and caterers might not take precautions when serving people with real allergies. This is because many customers claim to have allergies when they actually have food intolerances. Moira Austin from the Anaphylaxis Campaign said, "This can be fatal. If a caterer thinks someone just doesn't want to eat a certain food, they might not be careful enough."

A new guide says that most internet and shop-bought allergy tests are not based on science. These tests include home-testing kits that look for specific antibodies in the blood. However, research has shown that these antibodies do not necessarily mean someone has an allergy.

Other debunked tests include a mixture of acupuncture and homeopathy, hair follicle testing, and muscle testing. The guide says that these tests are pointless and can lead to people being misdiagnosed.

Paul Seddon, a consultant paediatric allergist, said, "I often see children who have been put on restricted diets because their parents think they have allergies based on fake tests." He added, "This needs to stop. We need to debunk these tests so that people can make informed decisions."

New Orleans, Louisiana, known for its vibrant nightlife, has banned indoor smoking in bars and clubs. This move is different from other cities because New Orleans relies heavily on tourism and promotes a "let the good times roll" attitude. The ban may have unique consequences due to the city's cultural ecosystem.

Since Hurricane Katrina in 2005, the city government has been trying to reduce noise levels by policing bars and nightclubs more strictly. Some bar owners are concerned that forcing smokers outside will increase tension between residents and businesses. Many of New Orleans' best bars and live music spots are located in quiet residential neighborhoods, where neighbors have learned to coexist.

Martha Wood, who lives next to a loud bar, says she won't complain about the noise because it was one of the reasons she bought her house. However, she's concerned that small infractions could lead to her business being shut down. Some bars have already gone smoke-free voluntarily, while others are worried about losing revenue.

Geoff Douville, owner of Lost Love Lounge, supports the ban and believes it will attract more customers who don't want to smell like smoke. He thinks the city's uniqueness, with its option to take drinks outside, makes the ban a great business opportunity. Councilwoman LaToya Cantrell, who introduced the ban, agrees that it can be a win-win situation if bar owners communicate with their communities and keep their clientele respectful.

The health department will handle warnings and fines for non-compliance, rather than the police department. Bar customers are encouraged to report any illegal smoking by filling out a form or calling 311. Some business owners are worried about noise complaints, but Douville is optimistic that the ban will work in his favor.

I had just arrived in the city after a long bus journey from New York and was tested on my language skills during the job interview.

As a reporter, I spent my days covering political rallies and nights coordinating news coverage of countries like El Salvador, Nicaragua, and Guatemala. I also reported on disasters such as fires, floods, and explosions. But I struggled with understanding numbers in Spanish, just like I did in English.

I would often get phone numbers wrong, waking up Mexican grandmothers at 2 am because I had misdialed a digit. My reports were also inaccurate - I would say there were many more victims than there actually were. For example, I reported that 83 people died in a fire when the actual number was 38.

I eventually got a call from my editor in Washington, who was frustrated with my mistakes. "Has no one ever told you that the death toll can't go down?" he asked. I realized then that numbers in another language were a challenge for me.

Greece is struggling with two major problems: an economic crisis and a deadly new drug called shisha, also known as the "cocaine of the poor". Shisha costs €2 or less per hit and is widely available, making it a killer that has spread rapidly across Greece.

Maria, a former heroin addict, describes shisha as the worst drug she's ever taken. "It burns your insides, makes you aggressive, and drives you mad," she says. Despite its dangers, many people are turning to shisha because it's cheap and easy to get.

The health authorities in Athens are already overwhelmed by budget cuts, and the shisha crisis is putting even more pressure on them. Shisha is a type of crystal meth that can cause users to become violent and lose control. It's often mixed with toxic substances like battery acid, engine oil, and shampoo.

Konstantinos, a drug addict, says that shisha makes him want to kill. "You can commit murder without even realizing it," he warns. Many users have died from taking shisha, which is spreading rapidly across Greece.

Charalampos Poulopoulos, the head of Kethea, an anti-drug center in Athens, believes that shisha is a symptom of the economic crisis. He calls it an "austerity drug" because dealers are producing cheap synthetic drugs to cater to people who can no longer afford more expensive highs.

The economic crisis has led to record levels of poverty and unemployment in Greece. Depression, drug abuse, and crime have increased dramatically, while prostitution has skyrocketed as a way for women to finance their addiction. Many sex workers engage in unprotected sex to make more money, which has led to an increase in pregnancies among addicts.

If food waste were reduced by just 25%, there would be enough food for everyone who is malnourished, according to the UN. Every year, 1.3 billion tonnes of food are wasted - about a third of all food produced. This includes 45% of fruit and vegetables, 35% of fish and seafood, 30% of cereals, 20% of dairy products, and 20% of meat. Meanwhile, 795 million people suffer from severe hunger.

The UN has identified food waste as one of the biggest challenges to achieving food security. By 2050, food production will need to increase by 60% to feed a growing global population. Reducing food waste would help ease the burden on resources.

Food waste is a global problem that affects different countries in different ways. In developing countries, there are high levels of "food loss" due to poor equipment and infrastructure. In wealthy countries, there are low levels of unintentional losses but high levels of "food waste", where consumers throw away food because they have bought too much or retailers reject it for aesthetic reasons.

In developed countries, 30-40% of all food purchased is thrown away, while in poorer countries only 5-16% of food is wasted. In Europe and North America, each person wastes 95-115kg of edible food per year, compared to just 6-11kg in sub-Saharan Africa and south and southeast Asia.

Goodfellow says it's unfair that bankers get big bonuses while he didn't make much money from his invention. He also feels frustrated that he's not seen as a good role model for inventors and engineers. His groundbreaking invention generated billions of pounds, but he got almost nothing.

There has been a long argument over who invented the ATM. In 2005, John Shepherd-Barron received an honor for services to banking as the "inventor of the automatic cash dispenser." However, the UK government now says it was Goodfellow who invented the ATM.

In the mid-1960s, Goodfellow worked as a development engineer and was asked to find a way for customers to withdraw cash from banks on Saturdays. He came up with a machine that would issue cash on demand to recognized customers. To make this work, he invented the PIN (personal identification number) and an associated coded token.

The token was a plastic card with holes punched in it. The patent documents described a system with a card reader and buttons mounted outside a bank. When a customer wanted to withdraw cash, they would insert their card and enter their PIN using the buttons.

Dr Ben Brabon from Edgehill University has a popular massive open online course (MOOC) on vampire fiction. He says some people take MOOCs just because they're free and fun. This is different from traditional university courses where students pay fees and have to meet certain requirements.

A recent survey suggests that over one million workers in Britain might be employed on zero-hours contracts. This is more than previously thought. The Chartered Institute of Personnel and Development (CIPD) surveyed over 1,000 employers to get these results.

Many people are now asking the government to investigate the use of these contracts. Some organizations, including retail chains and Buckingham Palace, have been criticized for using zero-hours contracts. These contracts do not guarantee work or pay each week. Workers on these contracts often do not receive holiday or sick pay and need permission to look for other jobs.

The CIPD found that 38% of workers on zero-hours contracts consider themselves full-time employees, working over 30 hours a week. One-third of voluntary sector employers and one in four public sector organizations use these contracts.

Peter Cheese from the CIPD said that there needs to be a closer look at what zero-hours contracts mean for both businesses and employees. He thinks this should include considering both the advantages and disadvantages.

Some companies, such as Sports Direct and Cineworld, have been criticized for using zero-hours contracts. Vidhya Alakeson from the Resolution Foundation said that if one million people are on zero-hours contracts, this would be a significant portion of the workforce. She thinks this issue can no longer be ignored as it affects only a small minority.

Some big organizations in the UK have been criticized for using these contracts. Workers on these contracts often don't get paid holidays or sick leave. They also need to ask permission before working for another company.

The survey also found that some industries use zero-hours contracts more than others. These include hotels, education, and healthcare.

A new report says that six-year-old children know more about digital technology than 45-year-old adults.
This is because many children are growing up with the internet and smartphones. They learn how to use these things before they can even talk.
Ofcom, a group that checks UK communications, did a study on this. They found out that children's communication habits are different from older people.
They gave 800 children and 2,000 adults a test called "digital quotient" or DQ. The test shows how much people know about digital things like tablets, smartphones, and the internet.
The results showed that six- to seven-year-old children scored an average of 98 on the test. Adults aged 45-49 scored an average of 96. Children aged 14-15 knew the most about digital technology, scoring an average of 113.
You can now take a short version of this test online and get your own DQ score. The website also gives advice on how to improve your digital knowledge and stay safe online.

The way children communicate with each other is very different from older people. Twenty years ago, teenagers spent hours talking on the phone. Now, children aged 12-15 spend only 3% of their communication time talking on the phone.
Most of the time, they send written messages or share photos and videos. Over 90% of their device time is spent sending messages through social media, WhatsApp, or text messages.

When they're not using their phones, children also watch TV differently. They spend half of their viewing time watching live TV, compared to 70% for adults. They like watching short video clips on YouTube or Facebook, and streaming content from Netflix or iTunes.

The visitors' centre at Donana National Park in southern Spain offers a breathtaking view: 200,000 hectares of wetlands crucial for Western Europe's birdlife. Every year, thousands of migratory birds from Africa rest here on their way to Britain and other parts of North-West Europe. The park is also home to some of Europe's rarest birds, including the Spanish imperial eagle.

However, this beautiful landscape is fragile. In 1998, a devastating environmental disaster occurred when two billion gallons of acidic water mixed with waste metals poured into the park from a nearby mine. This toxic spill killed over 25,000 fish and nearly 2,000 adult birds, chicks, eggs, and nests. The clean-up cost 90 million euros.

After this disaster, Spain invested 360 million euros to restore the landscape. Some areas that had been drained for farming were returned to their original wetland state. This process has been costly but positive.

Despite these efforts, Donana is still under threat. Plans are underway to build an oil pipeline and new hotels and golf courses, which would require large amounts of water. Soil erosion from nearby farms is also blocking the park's channels.

The biggest concern for conservationists is the recent decision to reopen the mine that caused the 1998 disaster. "This is Europe's most precious bird sanctuary," says Laurence Rose of the RSPB. "Reopening the mine would bring back the very cause of the disaster 16 years ago, which is extremely worrying."

The government says they will use new technology to make sure the mine doesn't harm the park. But others don't believe them. They think it's too big of a risk and could cause another disaster.

Doñana is a very special place with many birds and a beautiful landscape. Many tourists come to visit because of its unique wildlife. But if something goes wrong, it could be very bad for the environment.

Cities are great places to live, but they often have problems like pollution, traffic, and not enough green spaces. Here are ten unusual ideas to make cities better.

Pop-up parks
Many cities seem to be built for cars rather than people. A simple idea is to turn an empty car park into a temporary park. This idea started in San Francisco as an art project called PARK(ing). It has since spread around the world and includes temporary farms and ecology demonstrations. Every September, there's a day of action to celebrate this idea.

Underground bike storage
Not everyone in cities owns a car; many people prefer bikes. But where can you safely store them? A company in Tokyo has designed an underground bicycle park that is only seven meters wide but can hold 204 bikes. You can get your bike back by pressing a button, and it will be delivered to you in just 13 seconds.

Glow-in-the-dark trees
A Dutch designer-artist has invented a tree that glows in the dark. This bioluminescent plant uses DNA from glowing marine bacteria and could one day replace normal streetlights.

Energy-harvesting floors
In London, there's a special floor near an underground station that captures energy from people's footsteps and converts it into electricity to power the streetlights above. The company behind this idea has also installed similar systems at Heathrow Airport and other locations around the world.

Supertrees
Singapore's Gardens by the Bay features man-made trees up to 50 meters high. These steel-framed supertrees have flowers growing on them, absorb heat, collect rainwater, and provide ventilation for two large conservatories below. Some of these trees even have solar panels on their branches.

The man told his rescuers that he left Mexico for El Salvador in September 2012. His friend died at sea several months before. The man was wearing only underpants when they found him. He said he survived by catching turtles and birds. There were no fishing tools on the boat, but there was a turtle inside.

A Norwegian student named Ola Fjeldstad is doing research on the island where the man was found. She said, "His health isn't good, but it's getting better." The man's name is José Ivan. He had to stay in the 7.3-meter boat for a very long time.

The people who found José took him to another island to meet the mayor. The mayor called the government office in Majuro, the capital of the Marshall Islands. They said they need more information about José before he can go to the capital.

José is staying with a family on the island and getting food from them. He had a basic health check and was weak but okay. Ola Fjeldstad said, "We're giving him lots of water, and he's getting stronger."

A survival expert named Fraser Christian said that if José's story is true, it would be amazing. But it's not impossible to survive at sea for a long time. He said people can catch turtles or small fish with their hands.

The biggest dangers when you're lost at sea are cold weather and no drinking water.

Google has mapped many parts of the world, but it hasn't focused much on the Arctic region until now. The company is working on a big update to maps of the polar areas, which will help people understand life in these cold regions better.

The town of 7,000 people will be visible on Street View in July 2013. To map the area, the team walked on snow-covered roads and trails, some made of ice, which disappear during the short summer months. They also walked along a 15km road known as the Road to Nowhere, despite warnings about polar bears.
